Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can efficiently solve complex problems that demand memory and dynamic adjustments, like the Navigation problem, by utilizing their internal state to store and update information. Nevertheless, fully connected RNNs tend to be vulnerable to overfitting and may require substantial training data. We introduce locality masked RNNs (LM-RNNs), a variant that incorporates pruning and widening techniques to strike a balance between sparse models and increased capacity. Through analysis of three different problems – the XOR gate, the Navigation problem, and the 24-bit Memory problem – we have found that LM-RNNs can learn with significantly reduced parameters compared to fully connected RNNs, while also demonstrating improved generalization and sample efficiency. Notably, our results have also been optimized to minimize the practical impact of the Discrete Clopping problem (DCP), which arises from the application of discrete Fourier transforms to high-dimensional stochastic parameters, by limiting the number of sparse parameters to a multiple of the time step. We have found that this approach significantly reduces the required processing time. We anticipate that our developed methodology will be adaptable to a wide range of problem settings and complementary to existing work on pruning, widening, and other regularization techniques. Additionally, our work may be extended to other types of neural networks by incorporating an external memory module. We categorize nilpotent algebras by dimension with a focus on their commutative, commutative nilpotent and anticommutative properties. Our findings reveal the irreducibility of corresponding geometric spaces, allowing us to accurately calculate their dimensions and establish general families of algebras associated with each space. Additionally, we demonstrate how these results contribute to an understanding of the length of anticommutative algebras in further study. The support for our conclusions comes from explicit examples that demonstrate the applicability of our continuum moduli spaces to finite algebras, as well as the computation of the length for a specific anticommutative algebra in five variables. Based on these observations, we propose that the length of anticommutative algebras can be generalized to all anticommutative algebras of dimension five or more. Furthermore, we make inferences about the structures of commutative and commutative nilpotent algebras in dimensions five or more, utilizing the proven results for anticommutative algebras. These inferences suggest possible restrictions on the Philipson-Smyth length for these algebra types. The conclusions of this article open the door for the exploration of geometric properties of nilpotent algebras and their length variations through examples in dimensions five and above. resulting in slow implementation of the necessary societal changes to mitigate its effects.

Clinical symptoms recorded in unstructured doctor's notes are inaccessible for further use.
This problem can be resolved by using information extraction techniques capable of adapting to different medical settings and professionals. 
In this research, we address the issue of extracting symptoms by using pre-trained and fine-tuned models, trained on diverse patient data, medical institutions, and specialties. 
To enhance model versatility, we propose a new approach that uses'signal notes', a separate set of notes containing essential clinical information that can vary across settings and patients. 
We successfully applied this approach by using existing datasets from various hospitals, demonstrating that signal notes can improve model adaptability to new hospitals without requiring access to original data. 
Additionally, we explored ways to reduce dependence on external data by using pre-trained models and incorporating clinical context, including doctor's names and dates, to enhance performance. 
Ultimately, this research leads to the development of a highly adaptable system for extracting symptoms from diverse clinical notes. 
Results show that this approach allows models to shift from one hospital to another with only a few minor adjustments in accuracy. 
This breakthrough could accelerate the application of natural language processing in real-world medical settings.

Deep reinforcement learning stands out as a promising AI paradigm for instructing machines via environmental interaction and adaptive feedback. We've adopted this approach for autonomous driving, leveraging a simulated environment to fine-tune our algorithm's performance. The choice of supervised learning, which relies on manually annotated data, wouldn't be feasible for complex tasks like driving due to their scale and environmental constraints. To overcome this, we developed a neural network-driven method for instantaneously annotating camera frames. Using this system, we generated large quantities of annotated data to support our deep reinforcement learning algorithm, which we refined with the aid of a custom simulator. The results show that our combination of annotated data and reinforcement learning yields exceptional performance, surpassing that of models trained solely with annotated data in terms of accuracy and efficiency. The benefits of this approach extend to the generalization of our model to real-world scenarios, where it exhibits robust performance despite encountering unforeseen conditions during testing. The outcome of this study is a precise model capable of operating a vehicle with ease in a variety of real-world driving scenarios. In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal for an innovative, highly efficient SNN accelerator built with customizable, reconfigurable hardware blocks. Each block features a dual-core processor designed to process spikes and synapses, with an integrated block buffer providing dynamic, high-speed storage for incoming data. Additionally, a hierarchical access mechanism enables efficient communication between blocks, while a network of buffers also facilitates the event-driven processing of neural networks. Several experiments were conducted to validate the performance of this new accelerator, including a comprehensive comparison with existing chips, a detailed analysis of energy consumption in comparison to and in contrast with traditional AI networks, and a measurement of operational speed in terms of spikes per second for various neural network sizes. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that, in nearly all cases examined, the proposed SNN accelerator exhibited superior efficiency in terms of energy consumption, with also with significantly faster processing speeds in comparison to equivalent hardware-based deep learning systems. Specifically, it was observed that, for each arithmetic operation, our proposed device could handle up to 180 times more events per second, and consume up to 105 times less energy in comparison to alternative solutions. In conclusion, the proposed Spiking Neural Network hardware architecture, featuring event-driven processing, efficient spike and synapse processing, and modular design, presents a promising solution for widespread adoption of bio-realistic neural networks in various applications. Moreover, our findings indicate that, for most scenarios examined, this new architecture could offer substantial gains in processing speed and energy efficiency in comparison to traditional neural networks and existing SNN chips. To harness this potential, we developed Pando, a novel volunteer computing system based on declarative concurrent programming, and powered by JavaScript, WebRTC, and WebSockets. By employing a dynamic network of unreliable, volunteer-sourced personal devices and their browsers, Pando facilitates parallel execution of a function on multiple values, thus enhancing efficiency on compute-intensive applications like animation rendering and image processing. Furthermore, our approach leverages the widespread adoption of Web technologies to create a massive, global volunteer computing resource, surpassing existing systems in scale, flexibility, and ease of use. Experimental results demonstrate the robustness and reliability of Pando, even with large datasets and complex computation tasks. Moreover, with its potential for adaptation in diverse domains, Pando's source code is made available for community access and further development. Lastly, motivated by the spirit of collaborative volunteer computing first introduced by BOINC, we invite readers to join the Pando project and contribute their personal devices to support a wide range of charitable causes, as well as other Pando projects, promoting community engagement and social good. By leveraging the collective computational power of a global community, we can accomplish great things and make a meaningful social impact through volunteer computing. For instance, in the context of saluting Earth, a Pando project that utilizes a range of techniques including satellite data, 3D modeling, and visual effects to create a massive model of the planet, demonstrating its capacity to demonstrate global unity and promote social change through volunteer computing. With its capacity to process complex data sets of up to 1GB or more from sources like satellite imagery, a Pando project can be executed in under an hour using over 100 personal computers donated by a community of volunteers. And when completed, the result can be downloaded as a single 6MB file, thanks to Pando's efficiency. A computational method for resolving nonlinear eigenvalue problems is presented, using an approximating function derived from the eigenvalues of a modified eigenproblem equation. By utilizing a variable sampling process that focuses data collection on the areas most critical to solution resolution, this algorithm efficiently distributes resources. It then employs the collected information to produce approximations for the sought-after eigenvalues and eigenvectors through linear solving of various depression nonlinear eigenvalue problems. Recent advancements in the computation of eigenvalues and eigenvectors enable the solution of large-scale problems with complex structures. Such a strategy was successfully applied to the solution of a nonlinear eigenvalue problem arising in the analysis of micromechanical solids. Notably, even with only three degrees of freedom per wavelength, the method was able to yield accurate eigenfrequencies with a relative error of less than one percent. Future developments of this computational method will incorporate elements that facilitate the rapid identification of the particular solutions that are most relevant to the given problem parameters. Furthermore, improvements will be made to the algorithm's ability to produce high-accuracy solutions to multiple eigenvalues. Such enhancements will likely prove valuable in the solution of a broad range of nonlinear eigenvalue problems. For example, the authors anticipate that the method will be useful in the solution of eigenvalue problems that are sensitive to parameter variations common in structural engineering applications. Moreover, the future developments will likely be applicable to the solution of eigenvalue problems in other fields of study such as applied mechanics and electrical engineering. It is worth noting, however, that the method is currently only applicable to problems in the realm of real-valued solutions. By employing this equivalence, we obtain a detailed characterization of these transformations, yielding new insights and results in various areas, such as Krieger embeddings, survivor sets, Hausdorff dimensions, bifurcation sets, and badly approximable numbers. We show that certain classes of sets associated with these beta-transformations possess unique properties, specifically that they are winning in Schmidt games and have the countable intersection property. Furthermore, we compute the Hausdorff dimension of these sets, which we claim to be the correct values. We also investigate the probability that a randomly selected survivor set of a beta-transformation contains a hole at zero. To accomplish this, we establish a key lemma that enables us to define a family of conformal dynamical systems conforming to a group action and incorporate a zero-holed version of its associated shift map. We show that the probability of a zero-holed shift map containing a hole at zero is zero when the system's conformal exponent exceeds one. We apply this result to calculate the probability that a randomly selected survivor set of an intermediate beta-transformation incorporates a hole at zero. many fields but their complex predictions are difficult to interpret. A new approach,
Disentangled Attribution Curves, seamlessly decomposes these predictions into
clearer features that are easily understood. By applying this method to data from 224
breeds of dairy cattle, we successfully improved feature interpretation for
high-performing random forest models by demonstrating a notable reduction in the
number of necessary features. These features are now clearly defined and show a
stronger correlation with actual genetic outcomes, as evidenced by a higher area
under the receiver operating characteristic curve for predicting genetic traits. 
Furthermore, we found that using Disentangled Attribution Curves enhanced model
interpretability while maintaining high levels of accuracy in prediction tasks. 
These findings suggest that Disentangled Attribution Curves can be a valuable tool in
guiding feature selection and prioritizing important traits for future research and
development. Utility functions can be found on our website at
https://salimborji.github.io/Utilities/DAC.html. Researchers can access the used
dairy cattle data through the DLDD website (https://www.dldc.org/Project/DDL/). 
The developed method is available on the GitHub repository
https://github.com/salimborji/Disentangled_Attribution_Curves. A related paper has

Despite this setup, model parameter exchanges can potentially expose confidential information, necessitating novel approaches for mitigation. Recent proposals, rooted in concepts such as multi-party computation and homomorphic encryption, often come at a cost of significant computational overhead, rendering them unsuitable for practical application. This work presents an alternative solution by harnessing the capabilities of Trusted Execution Environments to safeguard data and model interactions, thereby enabling efficient and reliable federated learning across disparate systems. Using a two-phase training protocol, central server and edge device operations are decoupled, with the former responsible for executing training steps on the distributed dataset, while the latter performs model updates, both through local data processing, if necessary, and reliable two-way data exchange, to synchronize and maintain dataset consistency. Experimental results confirm the efficacy and practicality of this proposed approach, demonstrating its operational feasibility, computational efficiency, and data privacy integrity in diverse TEE environments. Furthermore, empirical evaluations, concerning both efficiency and data confidentiality aspects, establish this approach as a suitable choice for federated learning applications, given that TEEs are employed, even with existing technological limitations, in comparison to more resource-intensive solutions, requiring additional hardware for differential privacy, for example. The embedded systems industry is massive and ubiquitous, as controllers found in automobiles, home appliances, and industrial equipment are all examples of embedded systems. Interfacing external components such as sensors and actuators through various protocols is a common challenge faced by software developers when building and testing embedded systems. To address this issue, several companies provide virtual interfaces that emulate the behavior of external peripherals when connected to a host computer via USB or network cables. Although the use of these interfaces can simplify the development process, it does not guarantee that the finished software will behave as intended when deployed on the actual device. To bridge this gap, the proposed approach uses the features of the Python programming language to create tests that verify the correctness of C-based software by prototyping the external peripherals' functionality. This methodology is exemplified in a case study involving a controller area network (CAN) interface, which is a commonly used communication system in vehicles and industrial settings. The chosen virtual interface for this application is the CAN interface emulator provided by Microsemi, Inc. The proposed approach has been successfully implemented in a real-world project, where a test was written to verify the behavior of a C-based software routine using the Python programming language. As a result, the combination of Python and C languages enables the development of robust, high-performance software that is tailored to the specific requirements of embedded and real-time systems. To substantiate these claims, the proposed approach has been validated through experimentation, which includes quantitative measures of its effectiveness. These measures indicate that the proposed approach can significantly enhance code coverage, a key indicator of test effectiveness, which in this study increased from 20% to 90%. Consequently, the proposed approach can significantly accelerate the discovery of faults in embedded software, which in this study revealed a fault in the CAN software library when tested with the proposed approach. Finally, the proposed asymptotic complexity of the created test reveals its scalability for real-time applications. Specifically, the study shows that the combination of Python and C languages enables the development of robust, high-performance software that is capable of executing within a time frame of O(n), where n represents the number of messages in the CAN bus. In conclusion, the proposed approach offers a promising direction for research in the field of test-based verification of embedded software. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a system call filter, demands minimal computational resources and operates at speeds of several thousand operations per second. Our findings confirm that Timeloops is an effective and efficient tool for creating system call filters. As such, Timeloops is an ideal solution for use in deployment environments where strict security protocols are in place and high-speed deployment flexibility is desired. Galactic centers, including our own, can be challenging to study due to the overwhelming presence of the supermassive black hole. Current observational techniques allow us to probe no closer than ~0.1 parsecs to the center of a galaxy. Our innovative approach utilizes the difference in wavelength behavior of water vapor masers at parsec scales to disentangle their emission. This method is successfully demonstrated in our observation of the galaxy NGC 4258, where we are able to resolve near its center at an unprecedented distance of ~20 light years. Our data show that the star distribution around the black hole in NGC 4258 is smooth and undisturbed, maintaining its characteristic bar or peanut shape even at an extremely close range. Our findings will contribute to accurate estimates of the black hole's mass and the dynamics of the galaxy's inner region. This paper bridges the gap between compressed sensing and statistical learning, leveraging sparsity and structure to minimize the computational burden of learning tasks. By developing a family of compressive estimators, we achieve both efficient computation and optimal statistical performance, surpassing traditional methods in both speed and accuracy. Building on this insight, we create a general framework for tackling large-scale data analysis tasks, like high-dimensional regression and matrix estimation, by formulating new compressive estimators and developing fast, parallel optimization algorithms to maximize their utility. Central to our approach is the notion of compressive estimability, and we invest significant effort in identifying general conditions for successfully applying this framework across various estimation problems. Furthermore, we illustrate the practical applicability of our method by applying it to both synthetic and real-world data, where it consistently outperforms established techniques in both accuracy and speed. Overall, this research underscores the potential of compressive learning as a powerful tool for handling massive data sets by harnessing the dual benefits of computational efficiency and high statistical performance. This research may also serve as a reference for location planning, ensuring that new buildings in Indonesia do not obstruct or damage existing sundials, thus preserving these cultural heritage sites for the benefit of future generations. Ultimately, this study aspires to stimulate the revival of sundial construction and usage as both a tool for informal astronomical education and a means of promoting local culture. As part of these efforts, design innovations for modern sundials will be explored in the conclusion. Additionally, recommendations will be provided for integrating these historical timekeepers into formal astronomy education to maximize their educational value and effectiveness. This research in depth investigates the model of spherically symmetric polymer black holes, which was first introduced by Gambini, Olmedo, and Pullin within the framework of loop quantum gravity. We explored how in the GOP model the spacelike transition surface at the classical singularity replaces it. Utilizing transformations in the coordinates, the authors were able to extend the metric to the white hole region, which led to discovering that the structure of the quantum black hole bears resemblance to that of wormholes, with their radii equal to each other. Moreover, the authors found that not only is the throat, but also the horizons and the spatial infinities where the energy conditions are breached. Calculations of the Ricci and Kretschmann scalars at various locations further reinforced that the throat is indeed the most quantum region of the spacetime. Finally, the authors examined the impact of quantum effects on the quasinormal modes of massless scalar field, electromagnetic field, and axial gravitational perturbations, which was discovered to deviate significantly from their classical analogs due to the influence of quantum effects. We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. Additionally, the isothermal compressibility exhibits a temperature-independent behavior. These characteristics serve as a foundation for the development of a simplified model for the thermal screening of Coulomb interactions in doped graphene. This model can be employed to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility using approximate methods like RPA or via semi-analytical calculations using the Schwinger action approach for Dirac fermions. Both methods yield the same results, demonstrating strong agreement with recent experimental data obtained through THz spectroscopy. This theoretical framework may also be applied to the study of thermal screening in other two-dimensional Dirac materials and in hole-doped graphene. Additionally, we briefly explore the thermal properties of hole-doped graphene. Due to the mass-like term in the effective action for holes, the specific behavior observed in the thermal capacity may not entirely translate to this case. However, the thermal screening of Coulomb interactions in hole-doped graphene can still be investigated using the derived formula for dynamic density-density correlations. For the purpose of this study, the key difference between massless Dirac fermions in graphene and holes in graphene is the presence of a mass term, which significantly affects the thermal screening of Coulomb interactions. Consequently, while the present findings for thermal capacity and compressibility may not be accurate for hole-doped graphene, the proposed model for thermal screening is expected to provide a reliable representation of the underlying physics. Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech incorporates contextual acoustic features into each sentence, enabling a more detailed understanding of semantic relationships. Additionally, cross-sentence coarse-grained semantic features aid in the development of a natural prosody. Through augmenting masked acoustic features with contextual elements during training, MaskedSpeech outperformed baseline systems in expressiveness and naturalness. These improvements were further validated in objective evaluations. Specifically, the Panoctoid dataset was utilized to assess improvements in naturalness, while the VCTK dataset was used to assess expressiveness. As a result, MaskedSpeech achieved higher MOS scores in both datasets. Specifically, it outperformed the baseline system by 0.44 and 0.61 points in the VCTK and Panoctoid datasets, respectively. Furthermore, it achieved a higher correlation between MOS scores and mel cepstral distortion compared to the baseline system in the VCTK dataset. In terms of ID metrics, it outperformed the baseline system in F1 score, achieving 0.63 and 0.69 in the VCTK and Panoctild datasets, respectively. These results confirm the efficacy of MaskedSpeech in improving semantic and acoustic connections within paragraph-level speech synthesis. Furthermore, it offers a flexible framework for the synthesis of texts with varied levels of contextuality. Its potential applications extend to the generation of mission statements, company slogans, and other context-rich text types where enhanced naturalness and expressiveness can greatly benefit system performance. In terms of system efficiency, it requires minimal contextual information for training, allowing it to scale more effectively than other context-based synthesis systems. We've enhanced projection predictive inference by enabling efficient selection of variables and structures in models beyond those in the exponential family. By projecting predictive variables into a latent space, we have created a generalized framework that: 1) maintains the original model's integrity while performing variable selection, 2) accurately detects relevant structures and retains posterior uncertainties, and 3) extends its applicability to non-Gaussian models with Gaussian outputs. Notably, our approach offers improved performance in relevant model settings. We've developed a simulation tool to demystify the method's underlying mechanics and showcased its effectiveness with real-world data sets, outperforming existing methods in variable selection and predictive accuracy. The methodological discussions and code repositories for model fitting and inference are publicly available. \newline

Climate change communication is complicated by the proliferation of conspiracy theories, particularly those found online. This research investigates prevalent conspiracy theories regarding climate change by analyzing a significant Twitter dataset and applies a sophisticated stance detection technique. Our analysis focuses on whether such conspiracy theories are more widely shared by those who do not believe in climate change or those who do. Furthermore, we examine the most popular conspiracy theories, their variations with differing levels of climate change acceptance, and reveal that non-believers predominantly disseminate messages containing conspiracy theory-related keywords. Notably, all conspiracy theories are not equally prevalent. Our findings also highlight their implications for effective climate change communication strategies. The study's methodological innovations involve the use of stance detection, a machine learning algorithm that classifies climate change beliefs, and a transfer learning approach with word embeddings. We find that such spacetimes naturally incorporate geometric patterns suitable for describing irregular, periodically-distributed matter within the universe. We also establish mathematical proofs for their local representation, as well as the existence and uniqueness of the Einstein's equations under these specific spatial constraints. Notably, our research uncovers an interesting set of precise solutions, illustrating how these spacetimes can be used in cosmology to model a universe transitioning from homogenous, isotropic states in the early stages to more complex distributions with voids and matter peaks over time. We present our findings in a simplified form, showing that these spacetimes can be represented by a set of two functions, thereby facilitating the analysis of geometric structures and providing a framework for understanding cosmological scenarios with flat spacetimes. Moreover, our research highlights that these spacetimes can be observed in two forms, depending on the perspective of the observer, either as a Minkowski spacetime with no cosmological implications or as a de Sitter spacetime with essential cosmological significance, thereby underscoring the significance of the observer's role in cosmological theory. This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining the principles of image restoration and image segmentation. The integration of image restoration aspects enables the proposed model to effectively handle images corrupted by noise, blurriness, missing pixels, and varied color schemes. Specifically, this approach extends the influential Mumford-Shah model, allowing for improved segmentation of gray-scale and vector-valued images affected by noise, blurriness, or missing data. Our model can be efficiently optimized using the alternating minimization algorithm, which converges under minimal conditions. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior segmentation results, particularly on blurry images and those with missing pixel values, outperforming existing state-of-the-art segmentation models. Furthermore, the proposed method yields reliable frequency domain solutions, enhancing the quality of restored images. The model's performance has been rigorously evaluated using both synthetic and real-world images, showcasing its effectiveness in various imaging scenarios. The corresponding mathematical proofs, numerical implementation details, and additional test images can be found in the supplementary materials provided online. The proposed method will soon be made available through the MatLab repository on GitHub. A solar type-I noise storm is created by particle beams accelerated from active regions experiencing significant changes in their magnetic field configurations. These storms exhibit significant intensity fluctuations in very short time frames and on very short wavelengths. The dynamic evolution of these storm sources remains largely unstudied due to a lack of high-resolution imaging data in metrewave frequencies. In this research, a case of a minor solar flare associated with a noise storm is presented, and observations reveal two distinct phases of evolution in the storm's source parameters: stabilization and oscillation. The source underwent stabilization during its initial 5-minute oscillations before undergoing dynamic changes in the subsequent 15 minutes. By accounting for the changing viscosity, the model determines how mass accumulates onto the black hole over time. Initially, the model reveals that for a non-relativistic equation of state with adiabatic index $\Gamma$, the mass accretion rate reaches a steady state $ \dot{M} \simeq \frac{\delta \dot{M}_{\rm Edd}}{(3-\Delta)\tau^2} $. Here, $\delta$ represents a factor measuring how far the cloud's angular momentum disperses, while $\Delta$ equals $1/3$ for a specific equation of state and viscosity type, leading to a significantly reduced accretion rate. However, for fast radial transport of angular momentum, the mass accretion rate can approach the Eddington limit. Using a self-similar method to simplify the equations, two cases with either low or high viscosity were solved exactly. Furthermore, for a cloud of gas with both radial and angular transport of angular momentum, the mass accretion rate was found to lie between these two limiting situations. Finally, for a case with only radial transport, the mass accretion rate was found to be independent of time, while for the case with both radial and angular transport, it was dependent on time. In addition, for a case where the cloud's angular momentum is efficiently distributed, its accretion rate was found to be independent of time, indicating a previously undiscovered phase of mass accumulation. In contrast, for a more general situation, the mass accumulation rate was found to be time-dependent. A longstanding issue regarding massive star origins involves whether these stars always form within dense clusters and, if found in less crowded environments, if they inevitably moved there.  Recent advances in wide-scale photometric surveys enable us to detect massive stars outside of clusters.  This study involves examining the relatively isolated region of the Chamaeleontis cluster (approximately 5.5 degrees^2) using multi-wavelength data from photometric surveys.  This region contains numerous young stars located within and outside of clusters.  A sample of 122 candidate O or early B stars was compiled based on their spectral location on an Hertzsprung-Russell diagram and was further observed spectroscopically using the VLT/FORS2.  These candidates were found to have a range of spectral types from O3 to B5.  Seven of the 122 candidates were located outside of clusters and had a median distance of approximately 1.5 degrees from the cluster boundary.  Six of these seven stars were moving in a direction indicative of cluster membership.  This study includes new radial velocity measurements for eleven of these candidates, showing that eight of them have velocities consistent with cluster membership.  This suggests a high probability (80%) that these seven stars formed within the cluster.  This study provides new insights into massive star origins, indicating that these stars can also be found in less crowded environments associated with star-forming regions such as molecular clouds.  This suggests a lower ratio of low-mass stars to massive stars in these regions compared to dense clusters.  This variation in ratios may influence theories of massive star formation and the dispersal of these stars across the galaxy.  This study also raises questions about how these seven stars managed to leave the cluster and settle in less crowded environments.  This is a crucial problem that needs to be resolved in the future.  This study also discussed potential observational biases that can affect the identification of massive stars outside of clusters and proposed new strategies to improve the detection of these stars through improved photometric surveys and precise stellar radial velocity measurements.  This can lead to a more accurate understanding of the galactic massive star population.  This can shed new light on massive star origins, evolution and the galactic mass distribution.  This can also improve our understanding of massive star formation and dispersal across the galaxy.  This can improve our understanding of how these stars can be found in less crowded environments and whether these stars necessarily formed within dense clusters. The problem of enhancing such documents is referred to as handwritten document enhancement. In order to devise an effective enhancement technique, it is crucial to establish a comprehensive understanding of the visual characteristics present in handwritten documents. Although previous studies have made significant contributions to this goal, they are largely confined to binary images. To address this limitation, this study aims to develop an approach for improving general binary and grayscale image restoration methods, applying them to handwritten documents. To this end, we have created a large-scale dataset of enhanced binary and grayscale handwritten documents, marked with error measures to facilitate thorough testing and evaluation of existing image enhancement techniques. Our results show that by applying our proposed dataset and a modified version of the widely-used dark channel algorithm, significant improvements can be achieved across various metrics. Moreover, we have discovered that traditional techniques applied to our enhanced images have the potential to reach near-human accuracy levels. To support future research on handwritten document enhancement, we have made our dataset available for public download and also released the enhanced images as well as the source code for the employed method. In vehicular communications, the complex and dispersive nature of channels makes reliable channel estimation vital for optimal system performance, yet the IEEE 802.11p standard's limited pilots lead to inadequate channel tracking. As a result, conventional IEEE 802.11p estimators experience significant performance decline. To overcome these challenges, researchers suggest using IEEE 802.11ac pilots in combination with IEEE 802.11p signals. This allows for the utilization of more efficient IEEE 802.11ac estimation techniques, like the Super-IEEE 802.11p approach. However, accurately modeling IEEE 802.11p receiver functionality is essential to successfully combining the two signal types. Furthermore, a substantial number of pilot symbols in IEEE 802.11ac leads to efficient channel tracking. Consequently, the estimated channel can be utilized in long-term IEEE 802.11p systems, even with limited pilot availability. This paper showcases the modifications required for the Super-IEEE 802.11p approach to function in realistic scenarios with vehicle mobility and offers an extensive channel estimation evaluation, including simulations of practical scenarios combining IEEE 802.11p and IEEE 802.11ac. Additionally, this paper also addresses the difficulties and possible solutions in utilizing IEEE 802.11ac pilots for channel estimation, focusing on the critical design elements of vehicular communication systems. The results presented in this paper are part of a extensive campaign involving practical measurements in the Freeway scenario. Details of this campaign can be found in a companion document. Experimental outcomes confirm that the Super-IEEE 802.11p approach achieves superior performance in comparison to conventional IEEE 802.11p estimators. Moreover, this approach is capable of generating channel estimates even in scenarios where the available pilot signals are insufficient for precise estimation. Furthermore, this approach yields efficient results even in the Freeway scenario, showcasing promising performance despite significant interference and signal loss. Ultimately, this approach yields an acceptable level of performance even in the Urban scenario, serving as a viable option for practical application. In conclusion, this research suggests the Super-IEEE 802.11p approach as a feasible and efficient estimator for vehicular communication systems, capable of effectively estimating the complex channel characteristics in mobile scenarios utilizing IEEE 802.11ac pilots in combination with IEEE 802.11p signals. The significant performance improvement in comparison to conventional IEEE 802.11p estimators, along with the ability to effectively utilize IEEE 802.11ac pilot symbols, makes the Super-IEEE 802.11p approach an attractive solution

The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered interest within the machine learning community for a limited time. Colorization is particularly challenging due to its inherently high degrees of freedom; when presented with an image, multiple plausible color combinations exist, and there may be no single definitive solution. Another related issue is Single Image Super Resolution, a task that involves converting low-resolution images into higher-resolution versions. This research paper proposes a novel, deep learning-based approach to Single Image Super Resolution and automatic colorization. The core of this method is a multi-scale residual network that leverages the extraction of diverse features at different scales to achieve accurate upscaling and detailed enhancement. Additionally, this network is paired with a colorization module that utilizes global and local features, as well as semantic information derived from pre-trained ImageNet weights, to generate more natural and contextually relevant colors. The integration of these two tasks facilitates mutual reinforcement and enhances performance. Notably, the proposed approach outperforms existing methods on the Middlebury benchmark in terms of PSNR and SSIM scores and produces more realistic, visually pleasing results on single image super resolution tasks and automatic colorization examples. The method's source code will be made available on the GitHub platform. The dataset comprising 100 images used for training and validation, as well as the automatically colored images used for testing, can be accessed via the GitHub link as well. The ECFA Early Career Researcher's panel started representing the interests of young researchers within the ECFA community in January 2021. Throughout its first two years of operation, the panel developed its organizational framework, cooperated with ECFA by offering input and insights, and introduced several projects focused on comprehending and addressing the varied needs of young researchers. This report outlines the details of the panel's formation and operations as well as its engagement with numerous activities during its first two years of operation. It highlights the initiatives the panel has undertaken and the challenges it encountered in its role in representing the interests of young researchers. The report is organized into sections that detail the panel's formation and operations, its participation in various ECFA activities, its ongoing and planned projects, as well as a reflection on its first two years of operation and the future perspectives of the panel. 

Key achievements of the panel during its first two years of operation include:
* Developing an online survey to gather input from young researchers on their concerns and suggestions for improvement.
* Collaborating with the CERN Young Scientists Programme to understand the needs of young researchers.
* Participating in the CERN CDF programme to gather feedback from young researchers on their experiences.
* Starting CIPilot, an online training programme for young researchers to develop presentation and public speaking skills.
* Proposing the Young Researchers Working Group at FLARE2022, where it was officially recognized and its objectives were defined.
* Launching an online discussion forum for young researchers to discuss their concerns and share experiences.
* Preparing a report on career development for young researchers which is expected to be published in due course.

In the future, the panel plans to:
* Continue to gather input from young researchers through ongoing online discussions and surveys.
* Develop and implement training programmes to aid in career development.
* Cooperate with various committees within ECFA to address the needs of young researchers.
* Present its views on important topics to ECFA and the broader community.
* Keep promoting its activities and services to young researchers within the ECFA community.

To overcome this limitation, a specific alternative strategy was implemented.  Establishing the bias correction involves verifying the local asymptotic normality property and a specific Bahadur-Kiefer representation.  Developed within the context of a traditional asymptotic framework, this proposal appears to retain effectiveness in high-dimensional settings, as evidenced by simulation results.  Two real-world applications have demonstrated the practical utility of this estimator.  Compared to traditional methods, it has been shown to offer improved accuracy in estimating the mean absolute deviation.  In addition, this estimator has utility as a cross-validation tool, enabling researchers to select parameters that minimize prediction error. The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of graph expansion. While relation extraction identifies connections
between entities in a text, knowledge graph link prediction involves
predicting the most likely connection between two entities. By combining these
techniques, the proposed framework, RelEx-KGP, utilizes relation extraction
outputs to inform knowledge graph link prediction models, effectively guiding
the prediction towards more accurate results. Through its incorporation of the
relation extraction module, the framework enhances the integration of extracted
information, outperforming existing methods that directly utilize the existing
graph structure in link prediction experiments using the SemEVAL 2007 dataset. 
Additionally, the study highlights the significance of incorporating
entity context in the consideration of relation-specific extraction outcomes.

process of graph expansion. The source code for the RelEx-KGP framework is

The study's outcomes have significant implications for the development of theoretical binary formation processes and the construction of realistic stellar systems. The research could also contribute to detecting planets around binary stars by providing a theoretical framework for binary formation influenced by core mass. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its dissemination. By analyzing the factors contributing to the spread of rumors, we developed a mathematical model and used numerical simulations to evaluate the strategies for containment. Furthermore, we proposed an artificial neural network to predict whether a piece of information is a rumor or not. Experimental results showed that our model accurately identified rumors with high precision and our proposed neural network achieved an accuracy of 65.45% in identifying rumors. The findings of this study can guide efforts to control the spread of COVID-19-related misinformation and inform the development of future studies on online rumor research. Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they pose significant challenges due to their large size. Understanding the parameters within these networks is complicated by their complex, nonlinear behavior. Despite the complexity, researchers have discovered that neural networks contain 'lottery tickets' – smaller sub-networks that can be trained within hours to achieve comparable performance. However, there is limited information available about the existence of these sub-networks within transfer learning scenarios, particularly when the source and target domains differ. In this research, we investigate the existence of these sub-networks in such scenarios and introduce a new method that can identify and train a sub-network before the adaptation process even begins. Using this approach, we can improve the accuracy of fine-tuning and achieve superior results on seven out of nine benchmark datasets. Moreover, we can refine the adaptation process by identifying and training a sub-network in real-time. As a result, we experience accuracy enhancements of up to 4% using this approach. Furthermore, we identify key characteristics that influence the effectiveness of these sub-networks in transfer learning scenarios. Crucially, we can generalize these results by achieving enhanced performance on the tasks of sentiment analysis, question classification, and action classification using the DeepChat dataset. A novel prediction method, referred to as ProCS, enables fast and precise calculation of crucial chemical shift indicators in proteins, thereby determining the spatial arrangements of proteins. ProCS is calibrated with the results of high-level quantum mechanical calculations, achieving remarkable agreement in predicting the amide proton chemical shifts of a small protein with a minimal error margin of 0.25 ppm (high correlation coefficient of 0.94). Furthermore, in predicting the chemical shifts of a larger protein containing 109 residues, the method demonstrates great efficiency, taking only approximately 3 minutes to predict the shifts while achieving a high correlation coefficient of 0.96 and a mean absolute error of 0.11 ppm. This predicted shift data is then utilized to refine the protein structure, demonstrating improved accuracy over predictions derived from quantum mechanical calculations. Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures to choose unlabeled examples. However, model uncertainty-based methods are susceptible to outliers and diversity-based methods may overlook key information. To address this, we introduce a two-phase approach that simultaneously considers both uncertainty and diversity. First, we propose a pseudo-labeling technique to assign labels to a limited subset of samples based on uncertainty. Building on these labels, we design a network to generate synthetic labels for the remaining data. In the second phase, we select samples with the highest divergence from the model's distribution to supplement the labeled dataset. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on various benchmark datasets and architectures, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Notably, our approach achieves a performance comparable to supervised training with a significantly reduced number of labeled samples. These groupings, or partitions $\mathcal{P}_t$, split a continuously increasing set of items $\{1,2,\dots, Rt\}$. When time progresses to $t$, a fixed number of items $R$ are appended to this set; a fraction of these added items joins existing groups based on probabilities defined across different time intervals, initiating new subgroups separately from the ones that merged with existing groups. The goal of reward learning is to create an algorithm capable of adapting its behavior to optimize tasks by using humans as judges. Current approaches rely on human feedback by averaging multiple runs of the algorithm with varying parameters, treating human feedback as a definitive indicator of task completion. Nonetheless, this methodology is flawed because human feedback is often ambiguous, incomplete or misleading. To resolve these issues, we introduce a concept for learning optimal rewards through uncertain and contradictory human feedback. We also develop a novel framework known as C C R L (Critic-Based Reinforcement Learning) C R L (Candidate-Based Reinforcement Learning), which segregates the algorithm into two modules: a candidate generator and a critic. The former creates diverse action sequences, while the latter assesses these actions using human feedback in a comparative manner. By segregating these modules, we can ensure that the critic's evaluations are grounded in realistic expectations of the algorithm's behavior. Experimental results demonstrate that C C R L accurately identifies optimal rewards even in scenarios where human feedback is uncertain or contradictory. We also found that C C R L outperforms traditional methods when human feedback is reliable, as well as in a scenario where feedback is consistently correct. We call this phenomenon the "Silence is Gold" effect. Furthermore, the framework comes equipped with mechanisms for handling ambiguous feedback and an inbuilt predictor that informs the critic of potential outcomes. We demonstrate the applicability of C C R L in a sample application and provide an open-source implementation for those interested in applying this technique in practice. Ultimately, the C C R L framework presents an effective solution for reward learning in complex tasks with the involvement of humans. In addition, it offers an innovative approach for segregating the algorithm into comparative modules, grounded in realistic expectations of the algorithm's behavior. We hope that the ideas presented here will contribute to the development of more advanced algorithms in the future. In recent years, various experiments have demonstrated the efficient use of electric currents to steer artificial molecular motors built from transition metal compounds and organic molecules. Ab initio calculations have typically been conducted without incorporating the electric current. We address this limitation by presenting a revised density functional theory that accounts for the impact of electric currents on molecular systems. Our proposed method is applied to a specific motor consisting of a Sc-based compound and an organic molecule, which are separated by a dimerized covalent bond. Our findings indicate that electric currents flowing through the metal atom in the lower part of the motor lead to a resonant vibration of the motor at a specific frequency. This frequency matches the oscillation rate needed to power a motor as proposed by Brownian motor theories. We show that electric currents can trigger a motor's operation and suggest that this mechanism may be applicable to a wide range of molecular motors. Moreover, our method can be extended to simulate the behavior of molecular motors immersed in a solvent using a mean-field approximation. We use this approach to investigate the influence of electric currents on the motor's vibrational modes and find that electric currents can also affect the motor's rotational motion. In this study, we investigate the concept of general convolution by considering the set of all possible $n$-dimensional vectors from a finite domain $D$, where the elements of these vectors can take on values from $D$. A specific operation, denoted as $f$-Convolution, is defined for two $n$-dimensional vectors $x$ and $y$, where the result, $x \circ_y f$, takes the form of an $(n+1)$-dimensional vector. Given two functions, $f$ and $g$, defined over a domain $D$, we seek to compute the output of the $f$-Convolution operation for each possible $n$-dimensional vector, resulting in a new function, $f \circgy$. A straightforward approach for computing this output would involve a $O(|D|^n)$ time complexity, where $|D|$ denotes the size of the domain $D$. However, as demonstrated in the accompanying submission to arXiv, a more efficient algorithm exists with a time complexity of $O(|D|^3)$ when the elements of the domain $D$ can be represented as integers in the range of $0$ to $B-1$ for some integer $B$. In this follow-up study, we have modified the algorithm to facilitate computation when the domain elements can be represented as integers in the range of $0$ to $B-1$ for any positive integer value of $B$. In particular, the output of the $f$-Convolution operation is defined as an $(n+1)$-dimensional vector, where each element is computed as the sum of products of pairs from $x$ and $y$, where one element of each pair has come from $x$, and the other from $y$. It is worth noting that the sum of products of pairs can be efficiently computed using a hash-based approach, resulting in a new algorithm with a time complexity of $O((\frac{B}{b})^3)$, where $b$ is the size of a hash bucket. Our study re-examined the data from the HST STIS spectrum (1998) employing new retrieval techniques to estimate the atmospheric conditions of the dwarf. Utilizing a grid-based carbon-rich GDS model, we derived a mass of $51.0 \pm 2.8$ mass units for GJ 229B. The analysis indicated an atmosphere characterized by pressure of $0.75_{-0.13}$ to $1.16$ bars, with a best-fit temperature of $869_{-16}$ to $+23$ K. In modern research on data-driven systems, a primary focus lies on overcoming challenges presented by high-dimensional complexities, hidden system dynamics, and the presence of nonlinearity.  The dynamic mode decomposition technique has emerged as a key tool for creating models of data-driven systems, and recent advancements have expanded its scope to address these difficulties.  To tackle high-dimensional issues, the sparse extended dynamic mode decomposition method reduces dimensionality by employing sparse representation.  For hidden systems, conditional model averaging and extended dynamic mode decomposition are combined to create a probabilistic framework that accommodates uncertainty in both dynamics and data.  Furthermore, a deep learning-based framework for dynamic mode decomposition known as deep extended dynamic mode decomposition has been developed, capable of handling highly non-linear systems.  The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of these methods by using numerical simulations to illustrate their performance in various challenging scenarios.  The methods were found to maintain accuracy and stability even in difficult conditions, and outperformed traditional dynamic mode decomposition when these challenges arose.  The study further validates these methods through the analysis of a real-world application - the study of the movement of a spinning vortex in a laminar flow of fluid.  The methods were found to accurately model the complex dynamics of the system, and to be robust to variations in the data collected from the experiment.  The work highlights the potential for data-driven modelling of the natural world when the challenges of data sparsity, hidden systems and non-linearity are successfully addressed. Moreover, our findings underscore the significant evolutionary linkage between neutron stars and white dwarfs within stellar binary systems, particularly through the process of accretion-induced collapse. Furthermore, our results highlight the ongoing corollary challenge to the core collapse scenario posed by millisecond pulsar observations, emphasizing the need for evolutionary stellar models that align with astrophysical settings. Lastly, our investigation also examines potential avenues for further research in the field.

As the planet rapidly moves close to its star, its surface temperature jumps from 400K to over 1400K in a matter of hours during its closest approach. Observations using the James Webb Space Telescope will soon take advantage of this planet's extraordinary environment to study various aspects of its atmosphere. Accurate information about HD80606b's orbit is crucial to making the most out of these observations. Researchers have conducted in-depth analyses of the planet's transits on February 7, 2020, and December 7-8, 2021, in collaboration with the TESS spacecraft and a global network of amateur astronomers. A key goal in reinforcement learning is to invert a target outcome distribution, which can be achieved using end-effect drives to implement goal-oriented motor learning, even without an explicit predictive model. End-effect models utilize a straightforward statistical representation of policy effects, which serves as a substitute for more computationally intensive predictive models. In the past, end-effect models were used to learn a basic navigational task. In this research, we apply end-effect drives to a more complex task - a reaching exercise - and successfully use them to facilitate learning when the reach target is obscured from view. Additionally, we show that end-effect drives can be configured to implement a variety of techniques, including imitation learning and curiosity-driven exploration. This finding suggests end-effect drives could serve as a simple, efficient, and flexible tool for training robust, goal-oriented behaviors. Finally, we propose a novel framework, called Motor Reinforcement Learning, in which a robot's motor actions are seen as a means to modify the target distribution directly, thus inverting it to produce a desired effect. Within this framework, we show that end-effect drives can be used to implement a basic but essential concept in motor learning - the association between motor actions and their effects. Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse memory mechanisms to track navigation history but fail to account for the fraction of relevant information in their memories.
We propose the MemoNav system, which leverages a fractionated memory database to retain both local and global spatial memories.
The MemoNav system consists of three components: a goal feature extractor, a navigator, and a memory database.
The navigator is supported by two memory modules: short-term memory and long-term memory.
Short-term memory stores a fraction of navigational history with increasing recall rates as goals are achieved, ensuring only partial information of previous goals is retained.
Long-term memory is organized by environment region, with memories updated through a map construction algorithm that eliminates redundant goals.
The maintenance of long-term memory is controlled by an attention mechanism adjusting weighting factors based on goal relevance.
We evaluated MemoNav on a challenging dataset and our results indicate MemoNav outperforms existing methods with higher success rates and fewer navigator steps. Additionally, we found MemoNav effectively manages memory without exceeding 20% of the memory capacity. Our analysis shows MemoNav is capable of learning navigation strategies by successfully integrating short-term and long-term memories.

This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze the entanglement properties of IBC bosonic symmetry operators within the SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetry groups. By adopting a similarity transformed basis, we establish a relationship between operator dimensions and dual density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) quantities, thereby gaining insight into operator scaling. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that operator growth is connected to the scaling of Hilbert space, which in turn is linked to the scaling of entanglement. Using the entanglement spectrum, we probe deeper into operator properties and dissect their contributions to the total operator dimension. Our findings reveal that, for SU(1,1), essential and redundant degrees of freedom emerge at a certain scale, whereas all degrees of freedom are equally important at smaller scales. In contrast, for SU(2), essential degrees of freedom emerge only beyond a particular scale, with redundant degrees of freedom dominating the operator dimension at smaller scales. Using the naturally adapted basis, we show that these insights can be translated to the system's Lie algebra, where the action of generators on the symmetry sector defines a new order and scale-dependent structure. Our analysis sheds light on the intricate relationships among operator dimensions, density matrix renormalization, and the entanglement spectrum, thereby illuminating the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems. Additionally, our study paves the way for broader applications of quantum information tools in systems exhibiting operator growth. Furthermore, our results may inspire the creation of new, more efficient algorithms for density matrix renormalization and the development of novel, more efficient symmetries for quantum simulations. Lastly, our findings could be used to design and implement classical simulation methods that are adapted from quantum information principles. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest elements is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. We investigate how different definitions of beta_k relate to each other, how to calculate it, and what its maximum value can be. Ultimately we establish a set of rules that dictate the possible values of beta_k for any graph. We also look into how beta_k behaves for different types of regular graphs and examine some of the questions it raises. Deploying machine learning in practical scenarios can often present challenges,
mainly stemming from uninterpretable models, questionable reliance on imperfect
data, or offering a sole prediction outcome without considering various
probability outcomes.
  This study proposes the concept of Indecision Trees as a modification of the
existing Decision Trees model. These revised models are designed to learn under
conditions of uncertainty, draw conclusions in uncertain situations, produce
reliable probability distributions over potential labels, and be dissected into
clear, logical arguments that can be applied to other reasoning systems. With the
capacity to handle uncertainty, Indecision Trees can address issues of unclear
data and model the notion of confidence. Furthermore, Indecision Trees can
represent any classical Decision Tree, facilitating a seamless transition to
inductive reasoning. 
  The Indecision Trees model was tested on datasets from UCI and OpenStreetMap,
yielding promising results in comparison to Decision Trees and random forests, 
while also illustrating the potential for logical interpretation and inductive
reasoning. 
  This proposal initiates a novel line of research, opening the door for further
research into inductive reasoning on datasets, leveraging the advantages of tree-
structured models.

First, we translate the coverage report into a set of inquiry-based learning prompts that suggest additional tests based on previous student actions. We also created a natural language processing powered tool to provide these prompts even when a student's test suite lacks coverage. Second, the tool was designed to allow students to reflect on their test strategy by highlighting areas of the code that are not covered by their current test suites. We conducted an experiment involving 80 introductory students, where they worked on three programming assignments while receiving either the traditional or the new inquiry-based feedback. As a result, students who received the inquiry-based feedback wrote more effective test suites, as measured by the number of lines of code covered. Additionally, students who received this feedback displayed improved grades in a subsequent assignment and provided positive reviews of its usefulness. Based on these findings, we believe that the new approach can educate students on the importance of structured testing and ultimately lead to better test quality. To achieve this, we plan to integrate the new feedback method into testing educational tools used by these students. In domains requiring reliability or transparency, explainable AI is increasingly becoming essential for handling the unpredictability of black-box machine learning methods, particularly in healthcare and data protection regulations. However, standard visualizations often fall short due to their inability to differentiate between subtle feature variations or accurately represent the interplay between absent and present objects. This issue could be addressed by using qualitative representations that highlight specific object features, thus allowing for better interpretation and understanding. This research proposes ObjectINS, an Inference-by-Necessity System that utilizes user feedback to infer the presence or absence of objects in medical images and provides insights into the features that contributed to the classifier's decision. Evaluation on chest X-ray images revealed ObjectINS outperformed traditional methods, achieving an accuracy rate of 85.45% compared to 75.20% for the control group. Additionally, ObjectINS provided feature-level object classification at a 77.10% accuracy rate. These results demonstrate the potential for qualitative system representations to enhance the understanding of machine learning classifiers. Internet Service Providers have long requested that Content Providers contribute financially towards improving network infrastructure, with promises of better Quality of Service. This research examines profit-sharing agreements between a single Content Provider and multiple Internet Service Providers, with the Content Provider agreeing to split profits in exchange for enhanced service quality by the ISPs. To model these negotiations, we use a Stackelberg game, where the Content Provider decides the distribution of its profits and the ISPs determine their level of investment effort, while in another scenario, we look into how Content Providers and ISPs collaborate, with ISPs deciding on how to split the profits fairly through a Nash Bargaining model, resulting in improved outcomes for all parties. Numerical analysis shows that Content Provider-led initiatives can lead to suboptimal results, whereas collaborative efforts result in increased network quality and reduced inequality in profit distribution between Content Providers and ISPs. Furthermore, we have established that when Content Providers and ISPs work together, the split of profits is approximately equal, as it should be in perfect synergy. Finally, we have explored how changes in market parameters affect network quality, discovering that responses vary significantly between Content Provider-led and collaborative scenarios. Based on these findings, we recommend that profit-sharing agreements be a collaborative effort between all parties, as it yields superior results and promotes more efficient allocation of resources in network upgrades. Moreover, these results can serve as a foundation for future research into more intricate agreements involving more participants and the interplay between network upgrades and content provision. establishing an inclusive and welcoming environment for all students to
engage in mathematical study. In response to low diversity among majors, the
department initially attempted to address this through targeted programs aimed
at enhancing students' mathematical abilities and boosting their self-confidence.

within a predominantly homogeneous setting. Conversely, an anti-deficit
approach prioritizes creating an inclusive atmosphere that brings together
diverse groups to collaborate and thrive. This reflection showcases the
department's shift in strategy, outlining specific initiatives undertaken to
promote an inclusive environment and highlight lessons learned along the way.

inclusivity statements, starting an Inclusive Math Space, and establishing a
Diversity and Inclusion working group. Furthermore, we will present initial
findings from our 2020 survey to the mathematics community at large, aiming to
facilitate broader conversation on creating more inclusive departments across
the mathematical field. Ultimately, our ultimate goal is to craft a more
inclusive vision for the department, one that may serve as a model for the
mathematical community to follow.

Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their inability to understand the context of the content they've parsed out. Contextualizing extracted phrases proves difficult because current neural models, which rely heavily on extensive training data, often struggle to apply this context to text outside of their training samples. In our proposed framework, BAFQA, we tackle this challenge by using natural language inference capabilities to reconcile the discrepancy between the extracted phrases and the questions they're meant to answer. Since BAFQA requires extensive, high-quality semantic annotations for natural language inference, we utilize these annotations to train and refine our system through an iterative process involving both pre-training and fine-tuning stages. Experimental evaluations demonstrate BAFQA's effectiveness in extracting and contextualizing critical information from research papers, outperforming previous systems in this area. Additionally, our framework allows for the inference of semantic relationships between extracted phrases, which can be utilized for automatic summarization and to improve question answering systems through iterative revisions. ADHD is a widely prevalent psychiatric condition that has been challenging to diagnose accurately. The advancement in computational capabilities and machine learning methods has enabled researchers to investigate the use of resting-state fMRI imaging data for classifying ADHD. In contrast to prior studies, which often relied on the entire brain for classification, this study focused on pinpointing the essential regions for utilizing a deep learning model. By using rsfMRI data from the ADHD 200 global competition, the researchers employed leave-one-site-out cross-validation to derive a highly effective CNN model. Notably, the study found that using only selected regions of interest for training and testing achieved comparable accuracy without relying on all brain areas, indicating a potential simplification of subsequent investigations with rsfMRI data. The best-performing model demonstrated a 70.5% accuracy rate, surpassing the 66.2% achieved in the 2009 competition, and the source code is accessible on GitHub. Furthermore, the study analyzed and visualized the critical regions for ADHD diagnosis by implementing gradient-based importance weighting, which revealed that both left and right anterior cingulate regions play a significant role in diagnosing ADHD. The findings suggest that focusing solely on a limited set of brain areas can yield comparable or superior classification accuracy for ADHD using deep learning on rsfMRI data. This discovery may contribute to reducing computational requirements and make it more feasible for researchers to investigate and improve upon existing deep learning models for fMRI-based ADHD diagnosis. Additionally, identifying and localizing the essential brain regions for ADHD diagnosis can yield valuable insights into the underlying pathophysiology of the condition. To enhance the reliability and interpretability of deep learning models for fMRI-based ADHD diagnosis, the essential brain regions should be investigated for potential alterations in ADHD. Based on previous studies, it is hypothesized that the critical regions for ADHD identified in this study will exhibit significant differences in connectivity and functional characteristics between individuals with and without ADHD. The study's findings will be used to assess this hypothesis in subsequent research, which will examine and compare the functional characteristics of the critical regions for ADHD in two independent datasets. The resulting changes in ADHD-related critical regions will be visualized, and the study's findings will be disseminated through an interactive 3D map accessible to the public. The conclusions from this research will inform our understanding of how ADHD affects brain areas, which can inform the development of treatment strategies. The source code for replicating the critical region selection and diagnosis in this study is available on GitHub at: https://github.com/Chen-Hsiao-Hsien
