Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both humans and machines are necessary to establish acronym context. Human contributions encompass explicit definitions, such as inclusion in a glossary or explanation in a text, whereas machines rely on inference through contextual analysis within a text. Despite decades of research, achieving human-level acronym analysis remains an unresolved issue. This thesis addresses this challenge by investigating how humans comprehend acronyms and developing advanced machine learning models, incorporating both left and right contextual components, to enhance accuracy. The findings indicate that contextual analysis is crucial for accurate acronym analysis but relies on effective design of model architecture and selection of relevant contextual features. Furthermore, systems utilizing human-defined definitions and computational models can combine to achieve superior performance. As such, these research findings can be utilized to enhance the development of both machine-learning and knowledge-graph-based systems for acronym analysis. In addition, an open-source acronym analysis platform was created to facilitate collaboration and shared learning among researchers. This initiative led to the establishment of the A2C benchmark suite, comprising 407 acronyms, along with corresponding definitions and contextual examples, freely accessible at https://github.com/uwdatamining/AC2Benchmark. In a second research endeavor, a novel method for detecting and explaining complex academic concepts was developed. This approach recognizes concepts through their acronyms and provides contextual insights by analyzing associated papers. Using a combination of machine learning and human evaluation, 502 relevant concepts were identified, along with their definitions and analytical data, and made available at https://github.com/uwdatamining/Concepts. These initiatives are expected to foster collaborative research among scholars and pave the way for innovative solutions in acronym analysis. As such, I propose to utilize these research outcomes as the basis for future work in the development of advanced acronym analysis models that integrate multiple sources, including text, networks, and human input, to achieve superior performance. In addition, I suggest investigating the application of acronym analysis in related areas, such as the discovery of new acronyms and their embedding into knowledge graphs, and exploring the connection between acronym analysis and other complex information extraction tasks. Ultimately, I anticipate that the acronym analysis platform and associated datasets will serve as invaluable resources, empowering scholars to create innovative models for resolving the complex challenge of acronym analysis. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless storage capacity. Based on this realization, our system organizes data into a hierarchical framework consisting of tiers represented by base PCR primers and contains object identifiers in a separate complementary strand. We've demonstrated the feasibility of this concept through the construction of two large datasets totaling 7.6 gigabytes and demonstrated the scalability of our design by showcasing a single-tier storage segment capable of holding a 6-gigabyte dataset. Furthermore, our system has been enhanced with a data update protocol and a built-in quality-control system that detects and corrects errors arising from the experimental DNA synthesis, DNA extraction, sequencing, and sequencing analysis processes. We've found that, although errors do occur, they can be reliably corrected and that the overall sequence fidelity exceeds 99.99%, far surpassing the current capabilities of DNA sequencing technology. We anticipate that the integration of our DNA-storage system, complemented by ongoing advancements in DNA sequencing technology, will soon enable the practical application of this technology to large-scale data repositories. Additionally, our system has been made available to the public through an open-source platform. Topological insulators are notable for their exceptional electron transport properties. Characterized by protected surface states, they can be identified by a non-zero bulk spin Hall conductivity and surface states with dissipationless transport. Currently, a lack of understanding prevents the utilization of these properties in practical applications. Recent advancements have allowed us to model and study a specific interaction between a topological insulator and a superconductor. By creating a hybrid system consisting of a helical topological insulator and a superconductor with a magnetic exchange interaction, researchers have found that the topological insulator's surface can become gapped while still exhibiting a non-zero bulk spin Hall conductivity. Furthermore, due to the superconductor's influence, the topological insulator's surface states can transition into a non-local, current-flowing phenomenon known as Majorana modes. Our calculations demonstrate that when a voltage is applied to a hybrid system, the topological insulator's surface can display zero-energy Majorana modes while still conducting Hall current. By building on these findings, researchers suggest that these unique properties can be leveraged to create highly efficient generators and transformers. Moreover, the connection between the topological insulator's surface states and Majorana modes can be exploited to develop new, more efficient thermal devices. Ultimately, the practical applications of these devices will depend on the realization of this hybrid system and its confirmation as a topological insulator. If successful, this could lead to substantial breakthroughs in the fields of energy conversion and the use of Majorana modes in quantum computing. Conversely, further study may be required to fully understand and exploit the connection between topological insulators and superconductors. Based on initial results, it is possible to envision a future where these unique properties are used to develop innovative energy-harvesting devices and to explore the practical applications of Majorana modes in quantum computing. Moreover, the connection between the topological insulator's surface states and Majorana modes can potentially be exploited to develop novel thermal devices, thereby expanding the reach of topological insulators in quantum computing and communication. Nonetheless, more research is needed to confirm the practical usefulness of this hybrid system in generating energy and utilizing Majorana modes. Ultimately, the practical implications of these findings will depend on the successful demonstration of these concepts through experimentation. In oscillatory media, regions that oscillate faster than their surroundings can give rise to outgoing waves, which are crucial for synchronizing disparate parts of the system. This study investigates how these waves, initiated by pacemaker-like areas, contribute to global synchronization. Using numerical methods, we simulated a ring of coupled oscillators with modified pacemaker regions, whose activity was independent of the surrounding oscillators' frequency. Our findings reveal how these waves, consisting of localized pulses, facilitate synchronization across the ring. As the pacemaker region's modified area is diminished, global synchronization is still achieved, but only through a route involving the destabilization of a natural oscillatory pattern that initially hinders synchronization. Our results also illustrate how the ring transport mechanism can give rise to complex patterns, consisting of graceful periods, whose phases are mapped onto a different variable. This research offers insights into the role of pacemaker-generated waves in synchronization and extends the understanding of global synchronization to systems exhibiting frequency variability and temporal activity asymmetry. Furthermore, it is believed that the mechanisms explored here are applicable to a broader range of biological and physical systems. Lastly, the methodology employed is versatile and can be applied to the study of other systems featuring outgoing waves generated by localized regions of heightened activity.

Physicians' written assessments and interviews with patients, stored as unstructured clinical text notes (CTNs), have been analyzed by recent studies using machine learning techniques to forecast diagnoses based on CTNs, via International Classification of Diseases (ICD) coding. Although these studies demonstrate the effectiveness of future diagnostic predictions, they neglect the limitations and potential biases associated with the ICD coding system. To address these concerns, this research introduces a novel transformation technique for ICD coding, converting it into a scale-neutral coding system (SNS) by referencing the US Congress's findings on health data protection. Using the SNS, the researchers recoded 443 unique ICD-10 codes and uncovered 52 ambiguous codes that could lead to biased forecasting. Utilizing the revised coding system, the researchers reevaluated and compared the results of two datasets, showcasing the significance of clear coding standards on the predictive models and the need for improved data protection. Additionally, the researchers implemented a data protection policy to safeguard healthcare data from potential harm. The complete SNS coding system, along with the research findings, can be accessed via a public GitHub repository. Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth of computation time with dataset size. A shift towards quantum computing could potentially resolve this limitation, providing an alternative to current statistical models. We develop and test a quantum equivalent to the K-means clustering method on superconducting qubits, contrasting it to a previously implemented quantum support vector machine. Results indicate that our algorithm matches classical K-means performance in both clustering and classification tasks, achieving an impressive speedup of 35 times over its previous quantum counterpart. Moreover, our algorithm excelled in terms of runtime scalability as it efficiently handled increasing dataset sizes. We openly share the quantum algorithm source code to facilitate future developments of quantum machine learning. Additionally, we highlight potential applications for this algorithm across various fields. We also use this opportunity to discuss open challenges and future research opportunities in the emerging field of quantum machine learning. Recent research on transportation networks has highlighted the need to account for uncertainty and reliability by modeling the variability in traffic estimates. Demonstrating statistical equivalence on particular stopping points by analyzing 'branches' produced by these algorithms on complete graphs reveals that these algorithms can generate uniform spanning trees in tandem. This realization enables a faster, hybrid method that leverages the strengths of both algorithms to expedite uniform spanning tree generation in complete graphs. Furthermore, a novel, two-stage approach is developed to adapt and explore this hybrid strategy across a range of graph structures, showcasing its efficacy and efficiency in examples, such as transitive graphs, where it outperforms Wilson's algorithm by generating a uniform spanning tree 25% faster. The study's findings also underscore the importance of considering the interplay between algorithms to uncover innovative, high-performance methods. This work presents a comprehensive music dataset named MusicTM-Dataset that enhances cross-modal retrieval capabilities. Currently, a limited number of large-scale music datasets that incorporate multiple modalities exist. To address this gap, we have developed a dataset featuring three modalities: musical notes (one audio sequence), lyrics (another audio sequence), and metadata (text describing album information, artists, and songs). Noteably, existing datasets in the domain do not incorporate lyrics, making MusicTM-Dataset an invaluable resource. Utilizing the LYRICS-TO-NOTES dataset mentioned in the paper, a subset of MusicTM-Dataset's lyrics-notation pairs was used to establish a baseline model leveraging the LTN2L framework, and by pairing this with metadata, the dataset was expanded to encompass a tri-modal structure. Furthermore, a second subset of the dataset was derived from the Music Metadata Corpus, comprising lyrics, metadata, and hand-annotated noise patterns to represent unstable audio sequences. Ultimately, MusicTM-Dataset consists of 94,698 pairs of note-lyrics pairs, 481,715 lyrics-metadata pairs, and 46,481 noise-metadata pairs, situated at https://github.com/dsmtt/MusicTM-Dataset. A baseline model describing the cross-modal retrieval tasks based on this dataset can also be found at https://github.com/dsmtt/MusicTM-Dataset. However, adding variable refractive index significantly changes how we assess stability in the dark solitons. Notably, only isolated imaginary axis eigenvalues are found, and energy-based stability is applicable but doesn't work for small energy solitons due to the influence of boundary effects. Moreover, we find that in the small energy limit, dark solitons become unstable if they have any asymmetry in their phase profile. We've developed an innovative approach for designing stellarators with considerable versatility. Flexibility in this context refers to the range of rotational transform values the stellarator's magnetic axis can accommodate without compromising its quasisymmetry properties. Our method enhances design flexibility by taking into account coil placement during the modular coil design process, leveraging planar control coils and integrability objectives to improve quasisymmetry and nested flux surface volume. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by optimizing a coil set inspired by NCSX design, which not only surpasses the NCSX flux surface volume goal but also achieves quasisymmetry with arbitrary rotational transform values. Additionally, we've discovered that integrability objectives can be relaxed without jeopardizing quasisymmetry, enabling more versatile stellarator designs. We propose using the optimal coil module as a seed to guide neural network-based stellarator design, which can efficiently explore a broader parameter space. As a test case, we successfully designed a versatile stellarator with moderate ellipticity using this approach. Neural network predictions proved accurate for flexibility and quasisymmetry, but the networks struggled to reproduce the nested flux surface volume accurately. We anticipate that our method and neural network predictions will contribute to the ongoing stellarator design effort and open up new possibilities for flexible and efficient stellarator design. Furthermore, we suggest exploring an intermediate design strategy that balances versatility and integrability, which could be particularly beneficial for stellarator design in the quasi-axisymmetric regime. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, different finite element codes, solver configurations, and problem parameters are analyzed. Furthermore, the research introduces an innovative approach based on the kinematic decomposition of the Green-St. Venant strain tensor to enhance the accuracy of modeling heart muscle deformation. Results indicate that both BDDC and AMG methods successfully converge to a solution, however, the BDDC algorithm exhibits greater consistency and is less susceptible to grid class and solver parameter variations. In contrast, the AMG method performs well on a single-grid evaluation but converges less reliably across different grid classes. The research suggests that using an algebraic coarse problem can still yield desirable outcomes but ultimately falls behind the performance achieved with a balancing domain decomposition method. Nevertheless, further optimizations are proposed to boost the efficiency of the BDDC algorithm for potential application in future research. Additionally, the study sheds light on valuable insights for potential application in future research. Also presented is an open-source code for the project to facilitate replication by other researchers. In conclusion, the thesis contributes to the advancement of using BDDC/ALM methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on massive grid systems. Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic wave manipulation, notably in flat acoustic lenses and ultra-high frequency ultrasound imaging. This concept, however, has not yet been implemented at the MHz frequencies common in ultrasound imaging due to difficulties in fabricating complex microstructures. Advances in two-photon polymerization now enable precise manufacture of sub-wavelength structures in this frequency range. However, shrinking structures in size introduces another challenge, where increased thermoviscous effects lead to significant energy losses. This research innovates by integrating an optimized two-photon polymerization design for a micro acoustic metagrating with a novel finite-difference time-domain numerical model accounting for non-ideal properties. Together, they achieve an efficient transmission enhancement of 6dB across a 30 degree off-axis angle at 2.5MHz, far exceeding previous simulations. Experimental validation in a water-ultrasound-transducer setup confirms the design's functionality with a 5dB transmission gain over a 30 degree off-axis angle at 2.5MHz. This breakthrough demonstrates the manufacture and operation of the world's first polymer acoustic metagrating, overcoming previous limitations and opening new avenues in modern ultrasound imaging. Moreover, this research lays a foundational model capable of predicting nanoscale acoustic wave propagation, applicable to a broader spectrum of metamaterial designs. This could lead to innovations in advanced imaging techniques using phase quantization and acoustic wave manipulation across various frequency ranges. In conclusion, this study successfully integrates advanced manufacturing and numerical modeling techniques at the nanoscale to design a cutting-edge acoustic metagrating device. With its potential for transmission enhancement and point of sale functionality, this technology positions itself for significant impact in modern ultrasound imaging. More importantly, this research marks a significant breakthrough in the development of acoustic metagratings, while its general principles can be applied across various frequency ranges and applications. Ultimately, this research paves the way for the creative solution of engineering challenges through innovative design at the nanoscale. In particular, this research shows that two-photon polymerization can be effectively used in the creation of acoustic devices operating in the MHz frequency range. The outcomes of this study can inform the future standardization process of mobile IAB in 5G NR. An open-source simulation tool enables the replication of the findings and further investigation by the 5G community. As an example case, the authors assess mobile IAB performance in an urban environment with vehicles and fixed UEs. The analysis reveals that mobile IAB performance heavily relies on the used mobility models, enforcement of IAB downlink data traffic, and the applied packet control enablers. Despite notable advancements in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing 'open-world' problems common in healthcare and automation. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. To enhance generalizability without relying on expert input, our 'open-world' system proposes the use of interactive learning models that collectively accumulate experience and evolve over time through self-discovery. The system comprises a Hierarchy of Self-Learning Modules (HSLMs), each of which processes sensory input and retains information temporarily in Working Memory. These HSLMs are organized in a Modular System (MS) and interact with their surroundings through a Sensory Input System (SIS) and a Task Execution System (TES). The MS is trained using a Self-Supporting Learning Mechanism that facilitates self-improvement by distributing experience among the HSLMs and their interactions with the SIS and TES. Our study demonstrates the capacity of the open-world system to tackle complex and dynamic problems, such as playing the 'Button World' game in which agents discover rules and exceptions by interacting with their environment. Compared to reinforcement learning models, our system exhibits superior performance and increased robustness in adapting to unexpected situations. The long-term vision for this research involves addressing critical challenges in both artificial intelligence and cognitive psychology and potentially yields a more human-like intelligence by exploring how self-learning mechanisms can give rise to open-world learning and problem-solving through collaborative interaction and shared experience. Our work is a significant step towards developing a unified theory of learning and intelligence by drawing on insights from biology, neuroscience, and cognitive psychology to create a groundbreaking AI system. The velocity of these waves is directly proportional to their distance from the Couette flow. This finding significantly deviates from scenarios involving highly regular solutions in Gevrey spaces, where a damping mechanism prevents long-term perturbations. This research is particularly notable given recent (2020) findings by Buckingham and Bona-Jang that initially reported the existence of non-trivial travelling waves in 2D Euler equation, although their results were restricted to a more narrow parameter space and regularity level of $s=3/2$. Recent (2021) research by Deng further expanded on these findings to include an infinite number of possible travelling wave solutions. This new work can be seen as a refinement of these previous findings, expanding our understanding to include a broader class of solutions with lower regularity. Moreover, this new research demonstrates that these travelling waves can be observed over a longer duration when considering solutions with regularity level $s$ as low as $1/2$. The study also confirms that these solutions do not decay in time and are not confined to a finite area, given the absence of a positive constant in the equation for the square of their velocity. This new class of solutions is particularly significant given that they arise spontaneously from the Couette flow under very weak regularity constraints. The  COVID-19 pandemic, triggered by SARS-CoV-2 in 2020, was officially classified as a global health crisis by the WHO. As a result, the world is relying heavily on public health precautions such as social distancing measures to curb the virus spread and maintain the healthcare system functionality. With the isolation of communities, access to reliable information has become restricted. Consequently, the health minister in South Africa updates the public every day on COVID-19 infections, including affected individuals' demographic and travel details. Meanwhile, the National Institute for Communicable Diseases provides daily updates on testing numbers, case counts, and fatality rates via infographics but often fails to release patients' ages or other critical transmission metrics. Recognizing the need to effectively share COVID-19 data while maintaining individuals' anonymity, this research proposes an information-theoretic framework to evaluate the information leak in daily updates by the health minister. By applying this framework, which is based on well-established concepts in information theory, the study determines the upper limit on the amount of information that can be disclosed about each patient's demographic without compromising another individual's anonymity. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that the current disclosure of the health minister's information regarding infected individuals' provinces does not compromise another individual's anonymity but does reveal significant information about the virus transmission. Additionally, the research reveals that providing more province divisions would increase information leakage, while using alternative geographic divisions would still expose transmission information even after the virus transmission probability drops below a specified threshold. Based on these findings, the study recommends that the disclosure of the president's daily updates be modified to include only the total number of infections, infections in unspecified locations, and fatality rates while utilizing information theory to evaluate the information leak and provide useful insights into the virus spread. Lastly, the study suggests exploring alternative data disclosure methods such as quantized data, distribution-based disclosure, or releasing updates at intervals to minimize information leakage while maintaining public transparency. With the adoption of this framework, this research aims to contribute to the development of more effective data disclosure policies that balance both the release of valuable information and the minimization of information leakage while maintaining public transparency.  Both objectives are crucial in fighting the pandemic and should not be mutually exclusive. By combining these goals, this research can offer practical insights to inform data disclosure strategies that balance these competing demands in the context of COVID-19 data. Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally asserts that if subsets A and B, of size k, have a sumset whose size is minimal (specifically, at most 3k-4), then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this context, we explore situations where subsets A and B, of size k, can be defined over the integers modulo n, such that their sumset has a size of at most 3k-4. By doing so, we are able to deduce several corollaries regarding subsets, of size k, within the integers modulo n. These corollaries can be seen to imply Freiman's 3k-4 theorem for subsets of the integers. Furthermore, we identify and analyze one particular instance where subsets A and B, of size k, can be defined over the integers modulo n, such that their sumset has a size of at most 3k-4, yet they do not exhibit arithmetic progressions. In particular, we find that this is the case when A and B are both comprised of consecutive integers modulo n. We also demonstrate that Freiman's 3k-4 theorem can be derived from our findings regarding subsets, of size k, defined over the integers modulo n. Additionally, we identify and explore a novel application of Freiman's 3k-4 theorem itself. In this application, subsets A and B, of size k, can be assumed to have a sumset whose size exceeds 3k-4, and by doing so, we are able to deduce circumstances under which at least one of A or B will necessarily be seen to comprise consecutive integers modulo n. Additionally, our solution addresses current technical limitations by optimizing system performance through efficient knowledge graph processing and data storage. Our findings highlight the potential for deep learning applications on knowledge graphs, as well as the significance of integrating multiple data sources in retinal analysis, which could be extended to other medical contexts. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. Interestingly, only a small set of features accounts for most of the variations between patients with severe symptoms. Furthermore, when applied to an independent test dataset, the proposed features showed promise in distinguishing between patients with severe and mild COVID-19 symptoms. To facilitate the replication of the study, the code and models used in this research have been made publicly available. Additionally, a neural network was developed to predict lung area to minimize bias in patient selection for further analysis. With continued advancements in machine learning capabilities and expanding available datasets, future enhancements to this method will likely increase its accuracy in forecasting severe COVID-19 symptoms.  In the long term, this research may contribute to the development of an imaging-based decision support system to aid high-risk patient identification.  Ultimately, this system may enhance COVID-19 treatment by targeting high-risk patients.  Conversely, a limitation of this study is the reliance on biased patient datasets found in public repositories which may impact the general applicability of the findings.  Another limitation is the potential for complete lung area to indicate patients in critical condition who may experience complications in the future. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect predictions having extremely low probabilities. We introduced a novel algorithm to mitigate this issue by adjusting the proposal distribution according to each class's relative frequency. Evaluations on the HICO dataset demonstrated that our method significantly reduces false positive rates by eliminating extremely unlikely proposals. As a result, the performance of the model improves, with top-1 accuracy enhanced by 5.0% and top-5 accuracy by 6.3% in the detection task, and an 11.6% gain in the link prediction task. We also achieved a 3.6% increase in the link prediction task on the COCO-RT dataset. Notably, our method is fast, with a processing speed nearly 30 times faster than interaction networks, making it highly accessible and easily integratable into existing pipelines. We have made our code publicly available for reproduction. Further details can be found in our paper at https://github.com/SimKal/VRD-FP-Reweighting. A new measure, referred to as quantum correlation cost (QCC), quantifies the amount of quantum correlation employed in weak measurement procedures utilizing the trace norm. It's demonstrated that the QCC is directly linked to the trace-norm-based quantum discord (TQD) by a factor dependent on weak measurement strength. However, this measure only captures a portion of a quantum system's quantum nature. Furthermore, the total quantum correlation cannot be extracted through any series of weak measurements, no matter how numerous. Additionally, research highlights a key difference between the QCC and TQD in their handling of post-separation quantum correlations. In particular, these measures agree on the optimal decoy state resource density in quantum computation, whereas other studies have suggested a need for higher minimal resource densities based on the PLOD. In light of these results, the PLOD is re-evaluated and found to underestimate the total quantum correlation, and the use of entanglement of formation (Fo) as a benchmark reveals the connection between the QCC and Fo. Due to its computational intensity, the Fo is not widely utilized in the study of quantum information metrics. In contrast, the PLOD is favored for its computational feasibility. Nevertheless, research indicates the PLOD underestimates both the QCC and Fo, underscoring the superiority of the Fo in quantifying quantum correlation. Consequently, the Fo is suggested as a more accurate indicator of quantum correlation, and its known links to other information metrics provide a framework for their re-evaluation. In particular, the Fo's connection to the trace-norm-based quantum discord (TQD) reveals the TQD's suitability for the characterization of quantum enhancement in interference phenomena. In contrast, the quantum entanglement cost (QEC), which is a more conservative measure of quantum correlation, fails to capture the essential requirements for quantum enhancement in interference phenomena, as indicated by its comparison with the QCC. Therefore, the choice of metric depends on the desired level of precision in the characterization of quantum correlation, and these measures are found to be compatible in their handling of the bound entanglement. In particular, research indicates the QCC is unable to extract bound entanglement, and both the PLOD and TQD are in agreement on this aspect. Furthermore, the use of entanglement of formation (Fo) as a benchmark reveals the Fo's ability to extract bound entanglement, and its known links to other information metrics provide a framework for their re-evaluation. Capturing long-range relationships in scene understanding tasks is a crucial goal in computer vision. While CNNs excel in many applications, they have limitations in modelling global, structured relationships due to their localized nature. Graph Neural Networks have emerged as a promising alternative for tackling such tasks, but most GNNs are designed for static graph scenarios, falling short in addressing the dynamic nature of relationships in scenes. To bridge this gap, we introduce a new message passing framework called the Dynamic Graph Message Passing network, capable of modelling relationships across any distance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our DGMP framework through successful integration into a semantic segmentation task, outperforming existing methods and achieving state-of-the-art results on benchmark datasets. Notably, our approach exhibits particular success on Panoptic Segmentation, earning us a 69.3% mAP score. The code for this project is freely accessible on GitHub. https://github.com/Atteno/DGMP.git. This criticism has led some to suggest alternative methods. This research, however, takes a different approach, with a focus on evaluating the effectiveness of these techniques. Using a benchmark of 126 benchmark suites from various fields, this study analyzed the accuracy of CF and CFF in two scenarios: fixed-point MCM and bit-wise MCM. The results show that CF is suitable for applications requiring high precision, while CFF can safely eliminate unnecessary multiplications in most cases, with both techniques reliable in integer arithmetic and a statistical analysis indicating a virtually zero error rate. Additionally, this study found that both techniques can be modified to prevent over-folding, a common issue, while a new approach was also developed to further optimize MCM operations using machine learning and hardware acceleration. However, the specific characteristics and energy thresholds of this new physics remain unknown. It's probable that insights gleaned from LHC data will need supplementation with higher-energy electron-positron and muon colliders to thoroughly explore the findings. As a consequence, researchers of quantum field theories face a unique challenge in predicting the relative probabilities of different final states in these colliders and interpreting the data through the lens of theoretical models. This study aims to facilitate the adoption of advanced computing techniques in particle physics research, particularly in the context of lepton colliders operating at the TeV scale, for which detailed simulations of particle collisions require significant computational resources. To this end, the research involves splitting the complex task of particle collider simulation into a network of interconnected tasks that can be independently computed. This divide-and-conquer approach has two main benefits: it enables researchers to utilize more efficiently the computational power of high-performance computers with many processing cores, and it also allows the seamless integration of specialized task execution on dedicated hardware, such as graphics processing units. This computational framework has been implemented in a publicly available code and validated through the simulation of particle collisions at various energy levels in both quick bench-marking tests and more comprehensive applications, achieving a speedup of up to 150 times in the latter case. As a result, this method has become a reliable tool for the efficient simulation of quantum field theories in the context of colliders operating at the TeV scale. Furthermore, this research has laid the groundwork for future advancements in the computational simulation of particle physics experiments, and it is expected to facilitate advancements in the theoretical understanding of quantum field theories, the computation of particle collider data, and the forthcoming lepton colliders of the TeV scale. Additionally, this method has a broader application in the computational framework of the Standard Model, as well as in the forthcoming physics beyond the Standard Model. Lastly, the adoption of this approach in the simulation of particle physics experiments has opened up new avenues for the theoretical calculation of quantum field theories, the computation of particle collider data, and the forthcoming lepton colliders of the TeV scale. Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation and cut-greediness.

This study builds on their work by demonstrating that the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation and cut-greediness can be applied to a broader range of graph classes, including those with restrictive neighborhood properties. A key component of this study involves developing an algorithm for calculating small-set question answers, enabling more general use of the Sherali-Adams PTAS. An alternative approach using the László Fenyés effective independence complex also yields PTAS results for specific graph classes. Additionally, the study reveals significant insights into the László Fenyés complex's computational limitations. Moreover, the study demonstrates that the iterative rank rank principle cannot be applied to certain graph classes, including those with restricted neighborhood properties. Finally, the study shows that the László Fenyés complex's computational power is equivalent to the iterative rank rank principle on graph classes with restricted neighborhood properties. Partial results are also obtained for general graphs. These findings are the first to demonstrate the applicability of the Sherali-Adams PTAS to certain graph classes with restricted neighborhood properties, assuming the extended László Fenyés effective independence complex. In various object categorization tasks, particularly in visually complex conditions, it has been demonstrated that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can outperform feedforward models.  This research aimed to uncover the specific role of RNN recurrence in aiding object categorization.  We trained RNNs on an object categorization task and discovered through linear diagnostic analysis that auxiliary variables such as object position, orientation, and size are communicated through recurrence and contribute significantly to performance improvement.  This evidence confirms our hypothesis that auxiliary variables are utilized to optimize object categorization in cluttered environments.  We also developed an alternative, non-recurrent architecture that mimics RNN performance by incorporating additional training data containing diverse auxiliary variables.  Experiment results indicate that models utilizing this data achieve categorization success rates comparable to RNN models.  Interestingly, we observed that RNNs are capable of learning auxiliary variables even with a minimal number of training examples, unlike their non-recurrent counterparts.  This reveals a significant advantage of using RNNs for object categorization in cluttered environments.  Overall, our findings highlight the significance of auxiliary variables in object representation and suggest that RNN recurrence can facilitate their effective communication.  Additionally, our study shows that the auxiliary variables can be learned even with few examples, but may require additional guidance in the form of pre-defined categories.  Finally, our work also indicates that RNNs are not necessarily required to exploit auxiliary variables, but rather a model architecture that can efficiently communicate them effectively achieves optimal performance.  This research has far reaching implications for the field of computer vision, as it sheds light on the underlying mechanisms of category-level recognition in visually complex environments.  Additionally, our study also offers a novel method for communicating auxiliary variables that can guide the development of more advanced deep learning models in the future.  This knowledge can also be applied to biological systems to better understand how living beings utilize auxiliary variables to recognize objects in their surroundings.  This research is the first of its kind to explore the role of recurrence in communicating auxiliary variables in object categorization, as well as the first to utilize linear diagnostic analysis to investigate this phenomenon using RNNs, an innovative approach that holds much promise for the field of computer vision.  Furthermore, our study also demonstrates a novel method for using auxiliary variables that can guide the design of more efficient deep learning models in the future, as well as a promising new technique for exploring the biological mechanisms of object recognition in living beings. Social media platforms are facing significant problems due to the presence of toxic content like hate speech, off-color language, and misogyny. These difficulties have caught the attention of the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community, driving innovative research in the field. In this study, we report on the performance of our system, TOXIC2+, in the 2021 JFTR challenge. The competition focused on identifying toxic posts in both Arabic and English, with our team achieving remarkable results. Our Arabic team ranked first overall with an accuracy of 80.73%, and our English team secured second place with an accuracy of 94.44%. Our approach to tackling this challenge involved combining both traditional machine learning algorithms and advanced deep learning models, which we detail in this article. Additionally, we highlight the importance of having both language model and task-specific pre-training for achieving optimal results, as our success has demonstrated. Furthermore, our study indicates that the application of data augmentation can be beneficial, but only when used in conjunction with a pre-trained model. Otherwise, it can have a detrimental effect on performance. Lastly, we emphasize the need for more sophisticated features to enhance the overall accuracy of the toxicity detection task.

Designing effective collision avoidance systems for mobile robots remains a key challenge, particularly when accounting for the robot's spatial structure.
In this paper, we develop a novel control approach that leverages Control Barrier Functions and Quadratic Programming to enable safe navigation for mobile robotic arms around obstacles, factoring in their unique geometry.
Our proposed method successfully incorporates geometric constraints by converting them into control constraints, allowing for seamless integration with the robot's spatial structure.
Simulation results for both a simple rod and a complex robotic arm validate the method's efficiency and scalability, demonstrating its ability to adapt to varying levels of complexity without excessive computation time. Furthermore, we examine the impact of increasing complexity on performance using the Method of Moments. Our approach demonstrates a high degree of flexibility and can be applied to a wide range of geometric configurations with some computational adjustments. Future work will focus on applying this method to actual robotic platforms in real-time environments. 
The paper's contribution resides in its innovative solution to geometric collision avoidance that can be applied to complex robotic structures, outperforming current methods due to its lower computational requirements. Additionally, we provide crucial insights into the design of safe control systems through the adoption of Control Barrier Functions. Our research aims to simplify the development of collision avoidance systems for intricate robotic designs.

Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations. Furthermore, we establish a benchmark for comparison with existing methods with the aim of enhancing the capability of smart vehicles to navigate through different weather conditions. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based knowledge distillation, allowing a student model to be trained on the basis of its counterpart's decision-making processes rather than their internal workings. Since network outputs contain valuable information about the data and can be extracted after training, our method leverages these features to bypass dependence on the original network. Moreover, our technique also considers the retention of crucial information by introducing an additional loss function. Experimental results on ResNet, MobileNet, and EfficientNet architectures demonstrate that it can produce results comparable to traditional methods in terms of accuracy, while offering the advantage of extended network architecures compatibility. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two agents together in a collaborative environment. This innovative approach expands the scope of imitation learning applications by enabling agents to benefit from each other's expertise. Furthermore, we showcase the practical benefits of Co-IL by applying it to two challenging continuous control tasks, where it outperforms traditional reinforcement learning and achieves comparable results to state-of-the-art methods that utilize expert guidance. Additionally, we highlight the significant efficiency gains achieved through Co-IL. This groundbreaking research has the potential to revolutionize the field of imitation learning and pushes the boundaries of what is possible in efficient learning. This project tackles the complex problem of simultaneously monitoring the positions and shapes of hands and objects in a sequence of depth point cloud frames generated by an RGB-D sensor, wearing no markers. We present a novel network, called HandTrack, specifically designed for this challenge. By recognizing that hand joint tracking is essentially a continuous optimization process, we propose a solution as a continuous sequence of operations. To achieve this, our network is composed of a forward pass module that uses a unique normalization technique to standardize input representations, a backward pass module that utilizes differentiable trilinear interpolation for efficient feature propagation, and a residual module that facilitates smooth and stable performance. We also introduce a module that can learn and propagate spatial and temporal gradients to accurately track hand joints over time. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, outperforming existing hand tracking methods, especially in challenging scenarios involving fast and complex movements. A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units. Instead, a method is introduced that identifies interference caused by all units consistently across multiple replicates using the K-neighborhood interference model. Even with high replicates, models face challenges in determining the degree of influence (K) due to limited information. Furthermore, the method is applied to the well-documented Fourth Grade Teacher Experiment by Katz and Rosenman (1960), which demonstrates the method's applicability in analyzing existing data sets. Results indicate significant interference effects in the studied context involving teacher performance assessment. Implementations of the method are now available online.

This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically simulating quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates. The efficiency improvement stems from deriving a novel upper limit for the number of stabilizer states required to express $m$ copies of the magic state, $|T\rangle$. The findings reveal that a superposition of no more than $O(2^{\alpha m})$ stabilizer states can accurately represent $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$, where $\alpha\leq 0.3963$. This discovery supersedes the previous best-known estimate of $O(2^{\alpha m \log_2 m})$. This research investigates a cosmological model characterized by time-dependent fractional energy densities. The study, primarily theoretical, analyzes the implications of such a model, determining essential conditions under constraints. A real-world application of this model would require the total energy density to remain positive, a condition derived from the square root of a determinant formula. The inequality of this determinant with zero indicates a closed universe, whereas equality indicates a flat universe, and greater values indicate an expanding universe. The study also considers how fractional energy densities contribute to the universe's expansion, finding that they remain non-negative in an expanding universe. Furthermore, the model includes a condition that the fraction of matter or radiation within the universe does not exceed one, and in the absence of darkness, these limits are further constrained. The model's validity is also compared to the standard $\Lambda$CDM model using the difference in areas of spheres, and the results indicate that time-dependent fractional energy densities can provide insights into the universe's phase transitions. The study further explores the model's boundaries using phase diagrams, demonstrating the model's efficacy in describing both radiation-dominated and de Sitter phases. The model can be developed using various fractional calculus operators, and the application is anticipated to contribute to both mathematical and cosmological investigations. Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing implementations of SRAM-based TRNGs are hampered by reduced throughput, high energy consumption, and their inability to be integrated in ultra-large scale integrated circuits due to inefficient access methods. In this article, a novel access method is proposed that enhances randomness, increases the throughput, and lessens the energy consumption of SRAM-based TRNGs. The new access method is based on a linear search algorithm that expedites random number generation by locating the SRAM cell with the shortest access time. The article presents the proposed algorithm, a randomness evaluation method, and simulation results that demonstrate the performance of this new access method. Compared to the best current SRAM-based TRNG architecture, the proposed access method requires lower energy (83.33% less) and facilitates a faster data transfer rate (15.38% higher), thus making it more suitable for use in ultra-large scale integrated circuits. The proposed access method also yields high entropy of the generated random numbers (99.99%) and meets the standards for randomness in industrial applications. Furthermore, the article reveals that the TRNG entropy generation rate can be increased by reducing the clock period, although this may negatively affect the throughput and energy consumption. Consequently, the TRNG throughput and energy consumption must be balanced in accordance with the requirements for randomness and the intended application of the random numbers. In conclusion, the proposed access method offers superior performance in terms of randomness, throughput, and energy consumption, thus making it an attractive solution for modern designers. The proposed access method can be integrated in ultra-large scale integrated circuits with high efficiency, rendering it an attractive alternative among current SRAM-based TRNG architectures. In addition, the article presents novel concepts for the design of SRAM-based TRNGs, including randomness evaluation, access methods, and the relationship between access times and randomness. The article further suggests future improvements for SRAM-based TRNGs, including the utilization of error-correcting codes to further ensure the reliability of the generated random numbers. The properties of thin films made from metallic transition-metal oxides can be significantly different from their bulk counterparts. In this study, we simulate a monolayer of strontium vanadate grown on a substrate to investigate the thickness-induced metal-to-insulator transition. We found that two different terminations lead to the same insulating behavior at equilibrium but exhibit distinct behavior when doped or subjected to a gate voltage. Through many-body calculations, we revealed various nonlocal fluctuations resulting from antiferromagnetic, ferromagnetic, stripe, and checkerboard orbital ordering instabilities. By considering the role of orbital degrees of freedom, we explain how these instabilities emerge and demonstrate how ultra-thin film reconstruction and changes to coordination polyhedra result in unique properties. Our findings support further investigation into ultra-thin films of transition-metal oxides for new spintronics and memristor technologies. 2 pages, 2 figures. Presented at FMPESS2021. This study investigates the effects of information dissemination on cryptocurrency markets. Firstly, a cryptocurrency trading network is defined by employing cryptocurrencies as nodes and weekly price returns as edge weights. Secondly, the analysis shifts to daily price data, where a more intricate network is constructed using higher-order statistical dependencies. The findings of this study demonstrate that cryptocurrency networks exhibit distinct properties from conventional financial markets, characterized by highly clustered and nearly two-partite structures. Furthermore, our investigation reveals that stablecoins dominate the cryptocurrency network's core, while ethereal cryptocurrencies comprise the periphery. Thirdly, a measure of sentiment analogous to the bull sentiment index is calculated for each cryptocurrency. The results indicate an inverse correlation between the network's core's positive sentiment and its distance from the periphery. Finally, the effects of dissemination of positive sentiment on price returns are observed, where the periphery shows significant sensitivity to such influences. Notably, the research also identifies Binance as the dominant exchange platform driving price movements across the network. The study's findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the cryptocurrency market's dynamics. Additionally, the study's methodology has broader implications for analyzing price dependencies in complex systems. The study's results have important implications for both practitioners and researchers in the field of cryptocurrency. The source code and data used in this study are freely accessible on GitHub. Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  Techniques such as transfer learning and data augmentation have significantly improved the accuracy of state-of-the-art models in this domain.  Past research has explored the potential of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and variants like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) in automated essay grading, although these have largely been surpassed by recent developments using transformer architectures like BERT and RoBERTa.  This study investigates the capacity of BERT-based models to accurately score essays in a standardized test, considering factors such as model architecture, sentence encoding, and data availability.  It is part of the Collective Intelligence (CI) project at Harvard, aiming to leverage transfer learning and data augmentation for NLP tasks via advanced search capabilities.  While the BERT-based models used here outperformed their predecessors, they still fall short of human scores, underscoring the need for more efficient information retrieval and augmented data to support machine learning.  Potential future areas of research include incorporating multimodal models that integrate text and numerical data, as well as using generative models to create synthetic datasets, which could complement existing datasets to enhance machine learning.  Another promising area of exploration is the application of CI's capabilities to address bias in NLP models and datasets, with a view to developing more transparent and fair machine learning systems.  Overall, this study highlights the utility of BERT-based models for automated essay grading, while also emphasizing the necessity of continued research into more sophisticated machine learning models and more diverse, augmented datasets, both to enhance machine learning and to address broader social and ethical implications in NLP. We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that enhances the anonymity of transactions in decentralized cryptocurrencies. Our Delegated RingCT (DRC) scheme is a verifiable secret sharing-based solution, addressing the limitations of previous RingCT implementations that were vulnerable to disclosure of sensitive information. In this context, each participant in a transaction is regarded as a verifiable secret sharing node. Our DRC protocol comprises two stages: the blending stage and the delegation stage. During the blending stage, each participant shares and combines encrypted transaction details using verifiable auxiliary hash trees. Subsequently, an optional delegation stage allows participants to delegate computation of syrization and commitment hashes to a central node, ensuring the anonymity of transactions. Our DRC protocol is built upon the Delegated Proof of Stake (DPoS) consensus mechanism, with the DPoS leader acting as the central node for DRC calculations. Our DPoS-DRC hybrid system enhances the scalability and efficiency of the DRC protocol. Furthermore, our solution mitigates the drawbacks of previous RingCT implementations, which were prone to centralization and computational overload. In our experiments using DPoS-DRC, we demonstrated a notable improvement in transaction verification times, with an average decrease of 67.94% and 65.13% respectively, compared to the standard RingCT and RingCT with Delegated Proof of Work (DPoW) implementations. Additionally, our DPoS-DRC system exhibited superior performance in terms of scalability, with an increased number of transactions per second of 105.9/TSP (Transaction Per Second) and 104.6/TSP. In conclusion, our DPoS-DRC hybrid solution presents a superior and practical solution for maintaining the anonymity of transactions in decentralized cryptocurrencies while addressing the limitations of previous RingCT implementations. With its enhanced efficiency and transaction verification times nearly twice as good as the standard RingCT, our DPoS-DRC system presents a promising future for widespread adoption in decentralized cryptocurrencies. Our vision is for the DPoS-DRC to be employed in the Binance DRC charity project, utilizing our upgraded protocol as a decentralized and efficient solution for maintaining the anonymity of transactions in charitable transactions. Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these reductions can be implemented using threshold circuits with specific characteristics. Additionally, our research reveals that nearly all threshold circuit classes capable of solving approximate undirected Laplacian matrices are also capable of solving approximate symmetric diagonally dominant systems, a broader linear system class. Finally, we show that $\#ATH$ - the counting version of ATH - is not contained within any of the previously mentioned classes, providing a new benchmark for space-efficient solving of linear systems and potentially expanding the scope of applications for such solving techniques. Furthermore, the complexity of precisely solving undirected Laplacian matrices in the binary field is conserved when modified to involve random rounding - a property we term probabilistic threshold equivalence and demonstrate its significance through our results. Researchers have made the initial detection of three massive gauge bosons simultaneously produced in high-energy collisions between protons.  These collisions were performed at the CERN LHC with the CMS experiment's data set that contains 137 fb$^{-1}$ worth of information.  Separate searches for individual combinations of bosons, including W boson variations, have been done using several patterns of final particle arrangements.  Together, the signals for these processes indicate a cross-section of boson creation that is slightly higher than that predicted by the standard model, occurring 5.7 (expected to be 5.9) standard deviations above background noise.  Specifically, signals for individual W boson variations have a significance of around 3.3 to 3.4 standard deviations and the measured rates of boson creation are also recorded.  Furthermore, no significant signals were detected for boson combinations that include at least two W bosons.  These new findings are the most accurate to date of their kind.  Systematic searches for boson combinations have been done to better understand the behavior of the standard model at high energy levels.  In addition, constraints on theories beyond the standard model have been placed that involve non-resonant production of Z bosons accompanied by boson combinations.  Lastly, direct limits have also been set on the standard model's high energy behavior by looking at boson combinations with a specific arrangement of final particles.  These new findings improve previously existing ones with data from the 8 TeV run.  These new constraints on standard model behavior have been placed with data up to 13 TeV.  In particular, limits on the standard model's high energy behavior have been set with a minimum energy requirement of at least 3 TeV for the individual W boson variations, whereas the minimum energy requirement is at least 4 TeV for boson combinations, including variations of W boson signals.  In addition, theories beyond the standard model have been constrained that postulate a resonant production of the Z boson accompanied by boson combinations with similar minimum energy requirements. Previous foundational Hebrew NLP tasks have heavily relied on the 30-year-old Hebrew Treebank. This outdated single-source corpus lacks the diversity of modern Hebrew, found primarily on the web. This research paper addresses this issue by presenting a new, open-access UD Hebrew treebank. This corpus, created by sampling various topics from Hebrew Wikipedia, provides a much-needed upgrade to NLP's understanding of contemporary Hebrew. The project evaluates its own annotations, compares its results to those of the existing Hebrew Treebank, and makes the data available for the benefit of the NLP community. Additionally, this study conducts a thorough examination of the established UD guidelines using both human and automated assessments. This project aims to enhance the NLP's comprehension of spoken and written Hebrew across all levels. Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible. As research advances, diverse teams can create new models and data, leading to shared knowledge and collaboration opportunities. Nevertheless, a challenge persists in neural networks' tendency to 'forget' previous tasks after being retrained. This drawback restricts cooperative learning, since networks often need to perform new functions after initial training. Confronting this issue becomes critical, or the growing complexity of neural networks may hinder their application in mechanics and related fields. To address this problem, researchers have proposed various solutions, including data storage, regulation techniques, and lesson planning methods. A class of methods called 'lesson planning' involves strategically designing the training process to balance task and data management. In the field of mechanics, researchers have only applied a few examples of task-oriented training protocols. To address the general challenge of forgetting, we present a new training approach that allows a neural network to handle multiple types of data simultaneously. This method is called the multi-task training protocol, or MTP. We implemented MTP on a straightforward computer vision problem and compared its performance with standard techniques. The results indicate that MTP outperforms existing methods in maintaining performance on initial tasks and achieving comparable performance on new tasks. To validate our approach, we conducted experiments using synthetic data and compared the performance of a convolutional neural network on classification and regression tasks. The outcomes demonstrate the efficacy of MTP in supporting simultaneous training with diverse data sets. These experiments also illustrate how to apply this approach to handle various types of data in the field of mechanics and provide a blueprint for its use in cooperative learning projects. Finally, we present a pioneering example of using MTP in a complex application in solid mechanics, involving the prediction of material behavior from microstructure. This example showcases the potential of this approach in supporting cooperative learning projects in the field of mechanics. This collaboration enables researchers to apply MTP in their projects, along with other relevant tools. To validate the effectiveness of MTP in actual research projects, we conducted two case studies. Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of central nebulae, yet little is known about what happens when the initial, intricate structure of these formations disintegrates. To investigate the long-term effects of this process, we conducted 30 magnetohydrodynamic simulations of kiloparsec-scale, kiloparsec cold clouds under conditions typically seen in galaxy clusters. The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocabulary-independent speech system without transcription data, requiring the transformation of training data into acoustic units for test synthesis. This study explores identifying and modeling the fundamental acoustic units in speech, comprising both transient and steady-state regions. The transient regions are represented by phoneme-boundary sounds, modeled using HMM-CCM, and the steady-state regions by vowel-like sounds, modeled using HMM-GMM. Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle these nonlinearities efficiently. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are applied to determine the specific parameters of McCormick envelope relaxations, allowing us to leverage learned constraints across preceding stages, thus yielding better performance, faster solution times, and more interpretable outcomes. Our planner was thoroughly tested and validated through a variety of walking and climbing experiments on a 10 kg hexapod robot. We've made our source code available at https://github.com/tu-berlin-mp-r/eeo.

We have developed two overarching frameworks for identifying achievable resource transformations in diverse quantum resource theories. Our first theory encompasses a wide range of existing protocols, each with its unique set of resource- preserving operations. It utilizes a series of inequalities to determine the accessibility of a given state as a resource for achieving a target transformation. On the other hand, our second theory provides a unified description of geometric and linear programming methods used in quantum resource theories based on multiple resources. This approach demands that the intermediate states remain within the resource space and that the output states exceed the resource space in some defined manner. Applying these frameworks to the theories of quantum entanglement and quantum correlation has yielded previously undiscovered results. We have discovered new protocols for generating Bell-diagonal singlet correlations and have found the limiting point for transforming tripartite entanglement into correlated tripartite states through local operations. Furthermore, we have established the conditions under which the square root of the fidelity is used to calculate the resource cost in linear transformations of quantum resource theory. This reveals the underlying connection between geometric and linear programming methods used in such theories. We have also developed the necessary and sufficient conditions for the physical realization of these transformations and have derived dual inequalities that describe the achievable transformations in quantum resource theories. We have further found that the maximal achievable transformations in such theories are always found at the optimal solutions of the dual inequalities. This provides a significant advancement in the understanding of quantum resource theories and opens up fresh avenues for applying these theories to real-world applications. To solve the K-sparse sparsity-based compressive decomposition problem, we propose a new approach that incorporates a robustness mechanism into existing decentralized learning methods. By assuming a bounded distribution for model weights, we develop a comprehensive framework for robustness, leading to the creation of a robust decentralized learning algorithm (DR-DSGD) that incurs only a minimal computational overhead. DR-DSGD is implemented through a three-step process and is theoretically proven to converge at a rate of O(1/K), where K is the sparsity level. Notably, our results indicate that DR-DSGD requires significantly fewer communications (up to a factor of O(log K) fewer) while maintaining similar computational efficiency compared to traditional DSGD. We further examine the benefits of DR-DSGD in scenarios where data follows a mixture of uniform and Dirichlet distributions. Simulation experiments validate the theoretical claims and demonstrate the effectiveness of DR-DSGD in achieving superior communication efficiency. Furthermore, our method shows promising applications in handling label fluctuations and model weight biases in deep learning systems. Building upon these findings, we propose an extension, Empirical Bernstein DR-DSGD (ebDR-DSGD), which is theoretically proven to converge at a rate of O(1/√K), enhancing the robustness of decentralized learning in compressive decomposition problems. Moreover, ebDR-DSGD requires minimal computational resources and communicates more efficiently, with up to a factor of O(log K) fewer communications while maintaining similar computational efficiency compared to traditional DSGD. The tight-binding model, which simplifies complex material properties into localized basis states, is ideal for explaining how light interacts with matter. However, different choices for how electric fields influence these basis states can significantly impact the model's accuracy. While the velocity gauge is commonly used, it leads to unbounded, oscillating dipole moments that conflict with experimental observations. On the other hand, the dipole gauge offers a more stable and physically intuitive representation of electric interactions. Our study demonstrates that, within the tight-binding framework, the dipole gauge is compatible with both velocity and Ritz-gauge choices. Notably, the dipole gauge yields coherent results for non-polar optical transitions, unlike the velocity gauge used in a previous study. This success suggests the dipole gauge is an acceptable alternative to the velocity gauge when building simplified models of light-matter interaction. While the Ritz gauge may provide physically intuitive descriptions, the dipole gauge offers more versatile applications. Our findings are substantiated through numerical examples in silicon-based semiconductors. The boundary conditions used in these examples are consistent with experimental setups. The dipole gauge's stability also enables the exploration of interactions between multiple electric fields. Therefore, the dipole gauge is a more versatile choice for describing light-matter interactions within tight-binding models. The proposed expression of light-matter coupling could be adapted for use in machine learning-based models of light-matter interaction, particularly those incorporating gauge-invariant quantities. Furthermore, this new understanding of dipole, velocity, and Ritz gauges may facilitate the development of accurate and stable models of light-matter interaction. In a problem focused on category-level perception, we consider utilizing sensor data to identify and understand objects within specific categories despite variations within those categories. An active shape model, where organ models are applied to the organ topology, is used to define the search space for 3D pose and shape estimation. Our initial algorithm for handling category-level perception involves using a probabilistic framework to utilize probability density functions for category-specific and common poses, which are integrated with an iterative closest point algorithm. However, this method faces challenges with intra-class point clouds having significant within-class variations. Therefore, we introduce an alternative method in which intra-class variations are directly handled through a variation model. This model applies deformations to a reference shape to generate a distribution of likely shapes for a given pose. Both algorithms are tested using 30 different categories with a combination of synthetic and real-world point clouds. The results show that our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy for 3D pose and shape estimation. An example application of this approach is shown in self-driving cars, where we can use the information obtained to determine the type and configuration of loads within trailers. In addition, we provide a dataset with 3000 synthetic point clouds and 7000 real-point clouds along with the code for the algorithm at a public repository.
