A new statistical method is developed for basket trials to assess the effectiveness of a new treatment in multiple patient subgroups under one protocol. This approach uses Bayesian statistics to optimize sample size and allows information sharing between groups. We develop formulas to ensure each subgroup trial meets specified criteria, comparing the new treatment to a control, by clinically relevant standards. For subgroups with pre-defined similarities, we find the minimum required trial sizes simultaneously. Our approach resembles frequentist methods when there's no sharing of data. Notably, by allowing data borrowing, we find smaller trial sizes needed than traditional methods that don't share information. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach using two actual trials. Further simulations demonstrate our approach maintains accuracy in detecting positive results without increasing false positives. The code for implementing this approach is freely accessible online. We intend for this method to be a useful tool for designing trials treating multiple diseases with a single, new therapy. It is also expected to increase efficiency in clinical trials assessing novel treatments. We hope this development enhances the value of basket trials in medical research. Specifically, we've added a keypoint detector to the point cloud registration task, allowing the network to identify and prioritize relevant data points for alignment. Our keypoint detector is based on the network's intermediate representations, which are determined through training alongside traditional registration targets. Segmentation of unseen imaging modalities without manual labels presents significant difficulties due to the considerable time and resources needed for annotation. Current techniques typically address a novel modality either by fine-tuning a pre-trained model or by dividing the tasks into independent image translation and segmentation steps. In this study, a Cyclic Segmentation Generative Adversarial Network is proposed that simultaneously performs domain adaptation and object identification within a single unified structure. Apart from standard CycleGAN losses and supervisory signals from labeled source domain images, additional self-supervised objectives focusing on the segmentation are employed to optimize performance utilizing target domain images devoid of manual labels. Evaluations on the segmentation of neuronal nuclei using EM images and unlabeled ExM images confirm that the proposed CySGAN outperforms not only pre-trained models but also methods that execute domain adaptation followed by segmentation in sequence. Our proposed algorithm, Feature Mapping RNN, leverages key concepts in machine
learning, including parameter sharing, Radial Basis Function kernels, and
adversarial training, to develop a novel RNN architecture for generating future
video features and anticipating actions. By using only the initial video frames and
a reduced number of parameters, Feature Mapping RNN efficiently generates future
features, which are then used in a multi-layer perceptron to forecast actions.
During training, we use an adversarial approach to ensure that the generated features
are indistinguishable from actual future features. By integrating CM-RNN, which has a
compact and parameter-efficient structure, we achieve state-of-the-art performance on
the MultiTHUMOS action prediction benchmark. Furthermore, our model is highly
accessible and can be replicated with minimal computational resources. 
The code for Feature Mapping RNN can be found at: https://github.com/samsgm/FMRNN. 
The model has been tested and works effectively with Python 3.7 and TensorFlow 1.14.0.

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds with a normal homogeneous structure of four dimensions. Finally, as an application, we classify the deformations of the canonical connection on specific nearly G2-manifolds, including those of the product of a sphere with S^6 and an Aloff-Walliser space, as well as that of Hom(G2). A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a particular condition under the action of a conjugation operation. Specifically, $T$ can be said to be C-normal if there exists a conjugation operation $C$ on $H$ such that $TC^\ast CT = C^\ast T^\ast T$. In the context of function mappings, a self-map $\varphi$ of the open unit disc can be described using a linear fractional expression. This work investigates the conditions under which the composition operator $C_\varphi$ and weighted composition operator $W_{\psi, \varphi}$, where $\psi$ is another function, are both C-normal operators for specific conjugation operations $C$ and $\psi$. Key findings include the identification of particular functions $\psi$ and conjugation operations $C$ that make $W_{\psi, \varphi}$ a C-normal operator, as well as the observation that $C_\varphi$ is a C-normal operator when $\varphi$ meets certain conditions. Ultimately, this research determines the conditions under which $C_\varphi$ is a normal operator, finding that $C_\varphi$ is indeed a normal operator when $\varphi$ is an isometry, but otherwise only when $\varphi$ is a restricted isometry. This work is accompanied by illustrative examples and counter-examples that highlight the significance of these findings. As a result of this investigation, the class of C-normal composition operators and weighted composition operators has been refined, and a crucial condition has been identified for these operators to be C-normal. This condition states that the weight function $\psi$ must be such that its image under conjugation $\psi$ satisfies a particular condition, and is in fact a constant, for the operators to be C-normal. This result is further substantiated by examples of functions $\psi$ that satisfy this condition as well as others that do not. Additionally, this study demonstrates that the weighted composition operator $W_{\psi, \varphi}$ is a normal operator when both $\psi$ and $\varphi$ are automorphisms, but otherwise only when $\varphi$ is a restricted isometry. This is accompanied by a significant finding that $C_\varphi$ is a normal operator under the condition that its image under conjugation $\psi$ has a magnitude less than or equal to 1. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in predicting molecular properties, but their accuracy relies on the alignment of training and testing data. To address this limitation, we've developed a framework for understanding and addressing data misalignments in point cloud models. By analyzing how different transformations affect model performance, we discovered that most errors result from simple translations, rotations, and scalings. Based on this insight, we created the alignment network, a new component that learns to compensate for data misalignments. When added to existing point cloud models, the alignment network significantly improves overall performance and offers reliable predictions even from poorly aligned data, as evidenced by our results on a diverse dataset of molecular structures. Furthermore, we found that when used in conjunction with traditional data alignment methods, the alignment network can enhance their effectiveness, leading to faster convergence in optimization processes. We've shared our framework and accompanying tests on 808K molecules via open-source links.

However, in this study, an idealized ground sound model, rooted in elastodynamic theory, is used to determine under which conditions ground sound is perceivable. Mathematical analysis yields conditions for both normal and tangential vibrations of the ground surface. Furthermore, a computational model based on the finite element method provides numerical solutions for various types of impacts, including those with oblique incidence and non-negligible Poisson's ratios. Additionally, an experimental validation of the model was conducted, revealing that ground sound is more pronounced under certain parameters, such as when impacts occur at angles or with materials having higher Poisson's ratios, thereby supporting the model's analytical findings. These findings contribute to a greater understanding of ground sound synthesis in the context of impact sounds. A prevalent form of demonstrating Bell nonlocality known as the all-versus-nothing proof is presented without the use of inequalities. This concept consists of two main species, referred to as "always-type" and "sometimes-type", which have received significant research attention. Past studies on "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs have primarily involved perfect correlations from stabilizer states. This has led many to conclude that perfect correlations are the sole means of yielding "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs. Contrary to this prevailing notion, our study offers a "always-type" all-versus-nothing proof rooted in non-perfect correlations. This research aims to clarify an enduring misconception and potentially expands our understanding of Bell nonlocality. Additionally, our study contributes to the ongoing development of simpler verification methods for quantum systems. This new method employs weaker criteria than previous approaches, allowing for the demonstration of Bell nonlocality with fewer qubits. Specifically, our study shows that three-qubit states can exhibit Bell nonlocality, a phenomenon that was previously thought to require at least four qubits. This research further establishes that four-qubit states can exhibit Bell nonlocality with alignments, a phenomenon that was previously thought to be impossible. This discovery opens doors for future research into the generation of Bell nonlocality with fewer particles. Utilizing density functional theory, we've used first-principles calculations to investigate its electronic, vibrational, and superconducting properties. Contrary to expectations, however, the hydrogen boride system fails to achieve a significant metallic state and instead remains semiconducting, primarily due to strong hydrogen-boron ionic bonds. Further analysis also reveals an unusually high hydrogen influence on the system's phonon spectrum, resulting in an extremely low estimated superconducting critical temperature of approximately 0.3 K, if treated as a conventional hydrogen-doped material. In conclusion, while the hydrogen boride monolayer displays an alluring initial appearance, its poor metallization resistance renders it incapable of superconductivity. Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes.  Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective; in contrast, Arthur draws comparisons to the Lawvere-Kock-Bell framework, a non-Archimedean approach known as Smooth Infinitesimal Analysis (SIA). A critical examination of Arthur's comparison reveals significant misunderstandings regarding the nature of the continuous, polygons with an infinite number of sides, and infinitesimal quantities. Additionally, claims by Rabouin and Arthur, suggesting that Leibniz considered infinite quantities to be inherently contradictory, rely on an incorrect blending of Leibnizian concepts of bounded and unbounded infinites - a distinction previously noted by early Knobloch. Instead, a framework developed by Robinson may provide a more accurate account of Leibnizian calculus, which can be formalized using a conservative axiomatic system for infinitesimal analysis called SPOT. This formalisation covers concepts such as the bounded/unbounded distinction, a distinction between quantities that are or are not assigned to points is inherent in his work, and the continuity concept aligns more closely with the definition of SIA. As a result, a revised understanding of Leibnizian calculus reveals that many of its concepts are equivalent to those of SIA, a finding which can be attributed to Leibniz's adherence to the Principle of Sufficient Reason.  In doing so, this revised account addresses prior misinterpretations of Leibniz's mathematical methods while presenting a new, corrected picture of his mathematical processes. Moreover, this correction is substantiated by a formal, conservative extension of SIA to include a reasonable understanding of bounded and infinite quantities - a result of extending SIA to include a reasonable understanding of bounded and infinite quantities.  In addition to its relevance to the history of mathematics, this work is also relevant to contemporary mathematics, as it describes an established conservative extension of SIA to include a reasonable understanding of bounded and infinite quantities.  In particular, this extension is known as Extended Smooth Infinitesimal Analysis (ESIA), which can be found on the following website: https://www.logicmatters.net/2019/07/01/esia/ and associated blog posts https://www.logicmatters.net/2019/07/02/esia-derivation-1/ https://www.logicmatters.net/2019/07/03/esia-integration-2/

One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity, which severely hampers their performance. To mitigate this issue, researchers have developed techniques utilizing auxiliary information to supplement scarce user-item interaction data. Notably, several studies utilize user reviews to improve recommendation accuracy, as reviews provide more detailed user intent information than interaction data. Despite this, existing reviews-based methods are often plagued by issues, such as data sparsity, bias towards long-tail items, and the difficulty in accurately modeling user intent across various reviews. To address these challenges, we propose a novel framework that utilizes a review-based user intent model to capture intended items for each user. By implementing a matching mechanism to match intended items with actual interacted items, our framework achieves enhanced recommendation accuracy. Experimental evaluations on two real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of our proposed model over existing methods, particularly in scenarios involving data scarcity. Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. This follows from an expanded version of the WRT Conjecture established in [B Shriwise, arXiv 1703.01665 (2017)]. Furthermore, we demonstrate that unitarily invariant random matrices with discrete spectral distributions and a normalized trace are also asymptotically free. This result is complementary to a recent finding by Ayyangar and Tze [arXiv 1803.10316 (2019)]. Lastly, we show that the Haar measure on $U(N)$ is the only unitarily invariant probability measure on $U(N)$ that remains asymptotically free under all unitary transformations. This solution resolves the Conjecture proposed in [B Shriwise, arXiv 1703.01665 (2017)]. Relevant key words include free probability, WRT Conjecture, unitarily invariant, random matrices, asymptotic freeness. Long sequences in time-series data are critical for predicting system performance, detecting anomalies, and making predictive maintenance decisions in fields like healthcare and industrial systems. However, scaling these predictions to cover extended future timelines remains challenging due to the non-sparsity of forecasting models, high dimensionality, and lack of precise error metrics for direct optimization. Our solution, LongSeq2Seq, involves breaking down long sequences into manageable segments, forecasting these segments simultaneously using a memory-based approach, and ensuring consistency across consecutive forecasts through the incorporation of external constraints. This framework enables the processing of multiple time steps ahead in a single pass, reduces the required memory to a constant factor, and facilitates efficient training and testing phases. Our experiments on diverse real-world datasets for traffic, energy, healthcare, and sales analysis demonstrate the success of our novel framework, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods in many cases while remaining computationally efficient. In this case study, we examine the capabilities of the Big Bear Decibel-free Radio Telescope to detect such low-frequency fluctuations and establish that it can potentially serve as a bosonic dark matter detector. Our research examines how static strain influences the valley Hall effect in two-dimensional materials. We develop a theoretical model describing the strain's impact on the bands of these materials and derive a current direction that depends on the strain's pattern and orientation. By applying this model to silicene and graphene under specific strain conditions, we show that static strain can induce a valley Hall current without the need for an external magnetic field. Additionally, we reveal that the valley Hall response can be modified by adjusting the strain's amplitude. Furthermore, we identify a valley Hall effect in silicene but not in graphene, illustrating the significance of atomic details in material behavior. Finally, we explore the potential for valley Hall transport via terahertz radiation and suggest pathways for experimental verification and the realization of valley coherent devices. Moreover, we discuss how this research can be extended to three-dimensional topological insulators. Lastly, we outline potential future applications of valley Hall effect in low-dimensional materials, including the creation of valley valves and valves that operate at the terahertz scale. \end{document}

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. These decoders function seamlessly within existing quantum computing systems and have been put into practice, having actually been used to correct errors in a quantum computing protocol involving hundreds of qubits. This approach holds promise as a universal method for solving complex decoding problems across various quantum codes and may contribute to the development of more efficient and adaptable quantum computing hardware and software tools. Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome, applying this method is extremely difficult when dealing with larger states. Another approach is offered by quantum jump metrology, a method that extracts information by continuously monitoring an open quantum system and inducing correlations with the aid of quantum feedback control. This method is utilised to measure the optical parameter of a laser beam walking on a spin ring, a complex system influenced by random fluctuations, for which quantum tracking methods exhibit notable advantages over classical techniques, even when the quantum state is not highly entangled. Furthermore, our research demonstrates the feasibility of combining the concepts of quantum jump metrology and parametric amplification to increase precision by leveraging the characteristics of quantum jumps induced by quantum feedback, a discovery with the potential to revolutionise the measurement of physical parameters. Finally, open-system modelling reveals that the key to success lies in the controlled decay of the quantum system, enabling the development of new techniques for measuring the optical parameter of a laser beam, a discovery with significant implications for quantum metrology. This work has been documented in the research paper titled "Quantum jump metrology breaks the traditional bounds of precision while measuring the parameter of a laser beam" published in the journal "Science Advances". A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex penalty terms that can be difficult to optimize, as they either over- or under-penalize the model's predictions. 

We introduce an approach that begins with networks initialized using a comprehensive feature set, allowing even basic models to achieve improved performance. On one hand, this rich representation provides an effective starting point for the optimizer, while on the other hand, it incorporates a beneficial bias towards handling OoD scenarios.

This robust feature set is generated using the Rich Feature Construction (RFC) algorithm, also known as Bonsai, which comprises a sequence of iterative training episodes. Each episode is defined by a specific set of training examples, and the model is trained using these examples with an emphasis on preserving the features associated with the initial data points. Following each iteration, the model is re-initialized with its optimized parameters, which serves as the feature set for the subsequent training episode.

The key insight behind our approach is to recognize that the optimized parameters serve a dual purpose: they function as both the model's initial parameters and the features associated with the model. These features are beneficial in that they are biased towards the initial data points, while the model itself is trained using an alternative set of examples.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using two distinct scenarios. Firstly, in the case of a multi-class classification task with unknown class assignments for some examples, we utilize our approach to identify and exclude the anomalous examples. Secondly, in the scenario of a multi-task learning setup with a sequence of classification tasks, each with unknown labels for some examples, we utilize our approach to identify and exclude the anomalous examples for each task.

Research into the characteristics of neutrino oscillations using active neutrinos may also lead to discoveries about sterile neutrinos, specifically in their associated parameters. We investigate the potential of DUNE, a forthcoming experiment, in searching for sterile neutrinos with masses in the GeV range. Our findings suggest that, depending on the redshift at which sterile neutrinos appear in the early universe, DUNE may be able to detect them using either a superbeam or a wide-band beamline. Once detected, DUNE will be able to measure the mass and mixing of sterile neutrinos with a precision of approximately $10^{-3}$ eV for a neutrino mass gap of 10 meV or $10^{-4}$ eV for a neutrino mass gap of 100 meV. Furthermore, DUNE may be able to constrain the mixing of sterile states with masses in the GeV range, a region largely unexplored by current experiments. We also demonstrate that the characteristics of neutrino events detected by DUNE can be distinguished from various astrophysical neutrino sources using a likelihood-ratio test. Finally, we estimate that the accumulation of 10 kW/cm$^2$ cosmic neutrinos over a 10 km beam distance, along with a 3.2 $\mu$b/cm/cm photoelectric cross-section and a 30% reflection efficiency, will yield an event rate of $1.4 \times 10^{12}$ (GeV/mice)/T cm$^2$ cm, rendering the detection of sterile neutrinos highly probable. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles and compared against results from standard models that artificially lengthened collision time steps. Our approach yielded more realistic results and significantly reduced computational costs. Specifically, our method allowed for a 35% reduction in computational time without compromising accuracy. Our algorithm was also shown to have a low memory requirement, thus it can be easily incorporated into existing large-scale simulations of particle-based flows. Our simulation results also highlighted the influence of stretched collision time steps on particle movement and the formation of turbulent structures in fluids. Our research suggests that artificially lengthening collision time steps can lead to particle behavior that is too passive, especially when simulating sediment transport with long-term, complex movements. In contrast, our multiple-time-step integration algorithm produced results that are more in line with both experimental data and post-newtonian theories. Our method provides an innovative solution for efficiently simulating vast numbers of particle collisions in both fluid flow and complex sediment transport applications. Our algorithm has the potential to greatly expand the scope and practical applications of particle-based flow simulations. High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault-tolerant mechanisms to ensure reliable operation. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to employ checkpointing via in-process fencing to achieve this, by frequently saving the state of computations in memory and recovering from previous states in case of failures. However, the integration of in-process fencing into parallel applications of high performance is hindered by a problem known as the synchronization bottleneck, causing an excessive slowdown when compared to normal execution. This study proposes two synchronization algorithms suited for integration with in-process fencing: the first type involves a fence-based synchronization approach and the second type involves a thread management approach with reduced overhead. Both algorithms were tested and compared against normal execution and current best practices in a Fengyun-3 Global Atmospheric Model simulation, yielding the following results: the integration of both algorithms a) reduced synchronization overhead by 60% when using a fence-based approach and 63% when using a thread management approach, b) maintained perfect data consistency, c) increased synchronization overhead by an average of 2.4% when compared to normal execution, and d) outperformed current best practices in several key areas. In conclusion, both algorithms represent viable options for integrating in-process fencing into high-performance computing applications at the parallel level. Based on performance, the thread management algorithm is recommended for general use. Additionally, further research is suggested to refine and optimize both algorithms to meet the demands of emerging exascale computing systems. We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing the statistical properties of non-hierarchical three-body systems with corresponding theoretical models. By running and analyzing one million simulations for distinct sets of initial conditions, our findings provide comprehensive insights into escape probabilities, the distribution of masses that escape, and the dynamics of gravitionally bound systems. Notably, our data reveals that escape probabilities are influenced not only by the total mass of the secondary relative to the primary but also by the mass ratio and binding energy of the secondary, which are characteristics that cannot be accounted for by existing statistical theories. Moreover, our results confirm that there is no universally applicable mass function that describes all gravitionally bound systems, regardless of the primary's mass. Finally, while our experiment largely agrees with existing knowledge on the subject, it also suggests the existence of a mass range where the probability of smaller masses escaping within a given time frame is lower than predicted by linear statistical models. Conversely, for larger masses within this range, the probability of escaping is higher than expected. Further investigation is needed to clarify the non-linear aspects of these results. Additionally, the distribution of masses that escape does not conform to a single, universal function, which means that specifying the mass function relies on knowing the characteristics of the primary's mass. Interestingly, for equal-mass systems, the probability of escaping within a given time frame is significantly lower than predicted by linear statistical models, indicating a non-linear relationship between mass and probability. While dynamic analysis showed agreement with existing knowledge on the subject, it also highlights an area for further exploration, where cross-correlations between angular momentum distribution and the dynamics of gravitionally bound systems might offer insights into the systems' complexity. Overall, our results encourage the continuation of this experiment with greater depth to examine the what, when, and how of the escape in non-hierarchical three-body systems in more detail. Measurements of the nuclear modification factors of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons were made in collisions of lead ions at the Large Hadron Collider in 2015. These measurements were based on data from both lead-lead and proton-proton collisions, and were found to indicate a suppression of the more rapidly moving $\psi$(2S) mesons relative to the J/$\psi$ mesons. Additionally, measurements of the nuclear modification factors were also found to depend on transverse momentum and rapidity, and were greater in collisions that occurred at higher center-of-mass energy per nucleon. Furthermore, measurements of the nuclear modification factors were also found to indicate a suppression of the J/$\psi$ mesons in collisions of small colliding systems, including those involving permutterations of gold ions and charged particles in collisions of permutterations of lead ions. These findings, which were in agreement with theoretical models of medium-induced gluon radiation and with measurements made in collisions of smaller systems using these models, were used to explore the properties of quark-gluon plasma produced in high-energy nuclear collisions. We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of squeezing and displacement are identified that maintain over 99% state fidelity compared to a highly sensitive reference state, known as a compass state, which also exhibits equivalent variance in small shifts measurements. Both proposed and compass states display analogous behavior as average photon number changes. Notably, in practical applications, the compass state's minimal number variance when coherent amplitude is low may indicate its suitability for estimating damping parameters. Conversely, our proposed states are more versatile, potentially effective in a broader range of conditions. The potential for the proposed states to be generated with fewer photons, using fewer resources, is also explored. The investigation into this non-classical family of states could contribute to advancements in quantum estimation techniques.

Given that inversion symmetry and time reversal symmetry govern the total pseudo-angular momentum of the system, any break in this symmetry leads to a generation of a circular current of atoms. By adjusting the chemical potential, the total pseudo-angular momentum can be modified, allowing the phonon circular frequency to be adjusted. We are reassessing the significance of thermal fluctuations in incompressible fluid turbulence and determining their relevance on a particular scale. As earlier studies by Betchov and Truesdell, and by Kazantsev were overlooked, new findings require reevaluation of the problem's fundamental aspects. By considering the properties of random velocity fields in space, we arrive at a conclusion that the root-mean-square amplitude of thermal fluctuations reaches the Kolmogorov length only when the correlation scale exceeds the Batchelor scale, which is many orders of magnitude larger than the Kolmogorov length in highly turbulent flows. Consequently, thermal fluctuations are negligible compared to the overall turbulence in the free evolution of incompressible fluid flows. The significance of thermal fluctuations in the onset of dissipation in decaying turbulence, and in the behavior of rare, intense velocity fluctuations in the inertial range, is also discussed. It is found that thermal fluctuations can significantly alter the dynamics of very rare, intense velocity fluctuations in the inertial range, which may be relevant in experiments measuring the intermittency of turbulence. Furthermore, we show that the concept of thermal equilibrium is not directly applicable to the high Reynolds numbers regime of incompressible fluid turbulence. To assess thermal fluctuations in incompressible fluid turbulence, we consider three models - the model of Kolmogorov four-cascade, the model of dissipation, and the model of inertial range, each of which requires a different approach to determine the amplitude and spectral density of thermal fluctuations. It is found that the model of Kolmogorov four-cascade is not compatible with negative divergences of thermal fluctuations in the inertial range, while the models of dissipation and inertial range yield orders of magnitude larger thermal fluctuations compared to the batchelor scale. Finally, the amplitude and spectral density of thermal fluctuations, as well as the geometric distribution of thermal energy in the inertial range, are determined in the model of inertial range, which is characterized by a cascade of nonlocal, intermittent fluctuations, where the exponent of intermittency, -6/5, is derived from the balance between negative divergences and the Struerm-Lundquist billow structure. The findings of thermal fluctuations in the inertial range, where the amplitude and spectral density of thermal fluctuations are much larger than previously predicted, may be relevant in experiments measuring the intermittency of turbulence, while the model of inertial range, where thermal fluctuations are much larger than previously predicted, could be useful for understanding thermal fluctuations in various physical systems

By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018). Furthermore, this operational interpretation is instantiated with a sound proof of step-indexed Kripke model validity for the stochastic lambda calculus. Additionally, we investigate suitable notions of reflection correctness in the context of stochastic lambda calculus, taking into account weak and strong reflection properties. However, due to the inherent weakness resulting from the use of weak reflection, a strong reflection property cannot be proved to be correct, and a constructive alternative is proposed instead. Conversely, strong and weak correctness properties can be formally stated but prove to be inconsistent with sound interpretations, raising questions about the adequacy of reflection properties in the context of probabilistic code. Finally, we examine the relationship between cut-elimination in stochastic proof-theory and the adequacy of operational and denotational interpretations, establishing the adequacy of a previously introduced cut-free calculus (Delahaye et al., 2015) but finding limitations in generalizing this to other stochastic proof-theory frameworks due to the presence of unequal reasoning. Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead.  The challenge lies in environments that are modeled as Markov Decision Processes, and current imitation algorithms often require access to expert actions within the exact same environment as the imitating agent.  However, in scenarios where the state space is large and varied from one scenario to another, or when domains involve high setup costs, this becomes a significant issue.  Our work addresses these concerns by introducing an innovative method that leverages simulations to mimic expert behavior.  By extracting key features from diverse scenarios, the algorithm generates a framework to dispatch agents to different tasks while training.  The method also utilizes self-supervised learning to boost performance.  The method's efficacy has been demonstrated on two complex systems: a manufacturing system with a large state space and high setup cost, and a vehicle dispatch system with a large variety of scenario states.  Compared to other imitation algorithms, our method achieved lower feature error and improved performance.  The method's performance was also evaluated on these systems by replacing the expert actions with optimal reward functions, and the results showed similar outcomes. This method involves partial implications between binary variables, which can be constrained by parameters such as confidence and support levels. We delve into the concept of redundancy among association rules from a theoretical perspective. Each transaction in a dataset can be viewed as a logical statement, and we investigate existing notions of redundancy among association rules. We also introduce new definitions of redundancy, focusing on how generating sets of association rules can facilitate inference. These definitions yield a characterization of redundancy among full implication bases. Additionally, we explore the problem of determining whether an association rule is redundant or not, along with related decision problems. We demonstrate that in the general case, verifying whether an association rule is redundant or not is an NP-complete problem. However, we find that in the best-case scenario (when the database is transducible), verifying whether an association rule is redundant is an NP-complete problem but can be solved in polynomial time when the database is a hypergraph. Furthermore, we establish a characterization of redundancy among d-cyclic association rules. We also investigate how the concept of redundancy relates to the minimal generating hypergraph of a database. We conducted an in-depth examination of these structures, focusing on their spatial patterns, movement, chemical composition, and whether they are physically connected. By analyzing their kinematics, we determined that these structures are not integral objects but instead are dispersing throughout the galaxy. For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is labeled as entirely compatible or incompatible. Yet, this simplistic approach is impractical for real-world Outfit Maker apps where users must identify which specific items might clash with their created outfits. To address this limitation, we introduce the Visual InCompatibility TransfORmer (VICTOR) that's tailored to tackle two distinct challenges: quantifying an outfit's overall compatibility and pinpointing individual mismatched items. Leveraging a fashion-oriented language-image contrastive pre-training framework, we fine-tune VICTOR on a wide range of fashion visuals. We expand upon the Polyvore outfit benchmark, introducing a dataset dubbed Polyvore-MISFITs comprising imperfectly matched outfits, to train and test our proposed model. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our proposed VICTOR outperforms or matches state-of-the-art performance on the Polyvore dataset while achieving an impressive 88% reduction in computational requirements, striking an ideal balance between accuracy and efficiency. We publicly release the VICTOR implementation at https://github.com/stevejiais/victor. Additionally, an accompanying video can be found at https://youtu.be/7QimkH7f1fM. VICTOR's predicted mismatched items closely resemble human annotations in the Polyvore dataset, with an average similarity score of 65. We observe that VICTOR performs relatively well on visually simple outfits but lags behind human expectations in more complex scenarios. We hypothesize this limitation might be mitigated by incorporating more sophisticated visual region feature embeddings. We also hypothesize that VICTOR could be further enhanced by incorporating more human-like rules of visual compatibility such as color, type, and style-based constraints. We envision an ideal future outlook where VICTOR's predicted mismatched items closely resemble or even surpass human annotations in the Polyvore dataset. We anticipate this future outlook to be within reach if researchers develop more advanced models that can effectively translate the intricate rules of human visual compatibility into machine-friendly formats. The main challenge hindering the advancement of integrated gallium nitride electronics lies in its low hole mobility. In this investigation, a theoretical examination was conducted on the hole effective mass in undoped gallium nitride beneath a compressive strain of 2 kV/mm, applied in the z-direction. Three-dimensional simulations of the electronic structure were performed using the BerkeleyGW package, with the results showing significant enhancements in hole mobility - by a factor of 100 or more - when pairing gallium nitride with indium nitride, aluminum gallium nitride, or silicon. The underlying reason for this improvement stems from the altered band structure, caused by the artificial extension of the hole bands in gallium nitride. In specific, the artificial potential induced by the compressive strain pushes the heavy holes closer to the zone center, lessening their kinetic energy and thereby increasing mobility. Conversely, pairing gallium nitride with silicon results in a push away from the zone center for the light holes, thus enhancing their mobility. The theoretical findings suggest that strain-matched heterostructures have the potential to greatly improve the performance of gallium nitride field effect transistors. In particular, a surface mobility of 10,000 square per volt per meter is predicted for a gallium nitride transistor beneath a 2 kV/mm compressive strain, applied in the z-direction, when paired with silicon. In contrast, a surface mobility of 1,000 square per volt per meter is measured on unstrained gallium nitride at room temperature. Finally, a comparison with silicon shows that gallium nitride may offer superior mobility, provided it is paired with silicon, but not when paired with indium nitride or aluminum gallium nitride. The theoretical estimations indicate that strain-matched gallium nitride transistors could outperform silicon-based transistors around the year 2030, while falling short of predictions for indium nitride and aluminum gallium nitride materials systems. The underlying reason for this shortcoming lies in the lighter mass of the light holes in these materials, thus increasing their mobility. We also demonstrate that these approximation methods result in $P$ being a Hilbert-Schmidt operator, which has the beneficial consequence of enabling the computation of its square for any conditional expectation operator $P$. Despite this opportunity, previous research has given it little attention, and models developed to account for time frames often show no significant improvement over traditional models. Previous studies primarily focused on validating the concept of time frame awareness, and used simplistic designs to demonstrate this possibility, yet these studies also established a baseline of 0.79 APE on the FB15k dataset using the TransE model. Our work presents the initial results of integrating temporal contexts into knowledge graph embeddings, and achieving substantial improvements of 11.57%, 5.81%, and 6.79% in APE on the FB15k, FB15k-237, and WN18RR datasets, respectively, when compared to the state-of-the-art models. Furthermore, our models outperformed current standards in link prediction tasks on the FB15k and FB15k-237 datasets, and significantly reduced the training time by a factor of 7. Our methods comprise two strategies for incorporating temporal contexts: the direct strategy, based on a novel application of negative sampling, and an indirect strategy utilizing a temporal-aware model. In this research, we have examined the complex aspect of the Heavy Quark potential, focusing on its behavior at both zero and finite temperatures in the presence of a strong external magnetic field. Our findings indicate that, in a pure magnetic field, the heavy quark potential exhibits a linear sigma-like as well as a nonlinear plasmon-like behavior at low temperatures. Moreover, as the temperature reaches the quark confinement scale, the characteristic features of the heavy quark potential in a thermal medium become more pronounced. In addition to these observations, the dissociation of the heavy quarkonium states, specifically the bottomonium and charmonium, has been investigated at both zero and finite temperatures. Our results suggest that the heavy quarkonium states can dissociate due to both the thermal fluctuations and the influence of the magnetic field; in the case of the magnetic field's impact, this dissociation is most pronounced for the bottomonium states. Finally, the research highlights the potential applications of the heavy quark potential in the fields of nuclear and astrophysical science, particularly in the study of compact stars and magnetic field phenomena. We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer arbitrarily small local spectral expansion.

Our research involves creating high dimensional expanders with arbitrary local spectral expansion, and in doing so, we introduce two key concepts: firstly, we create 'approximate covering spaces' of high dimensional expanders, and secondly, we utilize these spaces to construct new high dimensional expanders; these concepts not only offer insights into the properties of high dimensional expanders but also help us identify potential limitations in the field of combinatorial complexity theory.

We also take note that our method of constructing high dimensional expanders shares a resemblance with the method used in the construction and application of expander graphs, and as a result, this similarity may indicate the presence of a broader universal theory that can be applied to combinatorial complexity theory. Furthermore, we believe that our 'approximate covering spaces' could be of interest in the field of geometric topology, and as a result, we propose the following question: is it possible to use our method to construct high dimensional expanders with arbitrary local spectral expansion? 

In terms of applications, we utilize our method of constructing high dimensional expanders to solve two long-standing problems - firstly, we provide a new and simplified proof for showing that sampling based testing is effective for properties of distributions that are far from uniform; secondly, we provide an alternative and simplified construction for almost linear sized constant local spectral high dimensional expanders. 

As an added bonus, we believe that our method of constructing high dimensional expanders, as well as our new concepts of 'approximate covering spaces' and'sample preserving maps', could be of interest in the broader fields of combinatorial complexity and theoretical computer science.

Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential for outstanding zero-shot performance through cleverly crafted natural language prompts. However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error. Consequently, there is a pressing need to determine which qualities of a prompt influence its efficacy. To this end, we have collected and standardized a diverse set of prompts designed for specific tasks and tested them on tasks for which they were not initially intended. due to interference from overlapping frequencies. Research using Rydberg 
atoms shows promise in MW radar and communications systems. Yet, the atoms are 
susceptible not only to desired signals but also to interference from 
atomic interactions and environmental noise. To resolve these challenges, we've 
successfully adapted a method using Rydberg atoms to sense multiple frequencies 
of MW electric fields. The technique relies on exchanging spin orientations of 
atoms via Rabi oscillations, using light from an LED that excites the atoms.

the ability to extract multiple frequencies of MW electric fields from complex 
signals, effectively unraveling the complex mathematical equations involved in 
the sensing process. This breakthrough "atomic" sensor offers unprecedented 
sensitivity in detecting MW electric fields, potentially revolutionizing the 
field and opening new avenues for scientific research and applications. From 
technical perspectives, this method can be applied to sensing MW radiation in 
various environments and is expected to improve low-frequency radar systems.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. Despite its rare occurrence, a similar phenomenon has been observed in another low-surface-brightness spiral galaxy, NGC 4605C, indicating that this is not an isolated event. Using a state-of-the-art hydrodynamic gas simulation, we investigated how gas is distributed in these galaxies, seeking an explanation for the unusual pattern of star formation in UGC 8839. Our study reveals that both the disk structure and the location of the HII region in UGC 8839 can be attributed to a low-mass dark halo that is too weak to influence the overall galaxy morphology. The presence of a dark halo, however, is not necessary to account for the star formation pattern in these galaxies, as a low surface mass density in the outer disk of UGC 8839, likely caused by a low gas fraction, can produce a similar effect. Nonetheless, a dark halo is not the only possible solution, and additional observations are required to confirm our findings. Furthermore, our research suggests that dark halos may not always influence the morphological appearance of galaxies, even if they have a significant impact on the distribution of the galaxy's baryonic mass. Additionally, our study highlights the need for more detailed simulations of gas dynamics in galaxy clusters, as the predicted star formation pattern in these galaxies does not always match the observed patterns. Ultimately, further research is required to understand the gas distribution in these galaxies, requiring both improved hydrodynamic simulations and more precise data from spectroscopic observations. An estimated lower bound has also been proposed for the Hausdorff dimension of its Julia set under a specific growth constraint. Furthermore, evidence suggests that a quasiregular map's Julia set likely lacks a smoothing phenomenon when viewed in a hyperbolic component context. Additionally, an approach for constructing specific fast escaping sets in 3D space has been outlined, as well as a method for identifying Julia sets that contain all directed approach paths in a given domain. These findings are supported by numerical 3D visualizations of Julia sets. Lastly, an unconfirmed conjecture suggests that the Hausdorff dimension of a quasiregular map's Julia set may always be exactly 3. This research introduces novel technical tools, including a formula for calculating the Hausdorff dimension of a set that is accessible to 3D visualization, as well as a formula for estimating the Hausdorff dimension of sets derived from directional trajectories in a domain. These tools rely on the concept of charge distribution to determine the Hausdorff dimension of associated clusters. It is also demonstrated that the proposed lower bound for the Hausdorff dimension of a Julia set does not apply to a map that meets the Silvestre condition, leading to the conclusion that the map that meets the Silvestre condition has a Julia set with a Hausdorff dimension of exactly 3. Furthermore, a study on the relationship between the map's growth rate and the Hausdorff dimension of its fast escaping set revealed that a fast-growing map has a Hausdorff dimension of at most 1, while a slowly-growing map may have a Hausdorff dimension greater than 3. Using the Spectroscopic Investigation of Interstellar Medium project's data, we determine the 21 cm line intensity observed from gravitationally driven upper atmosphere emissions on Mars as observed by MAVEN. We calculate a mean of 80.3 sfu with a standard deviation of 453.6 sfu. Notably, gravitationally induced gravity waves in the upper atmosphere correlate with Martian solar wind interactions, weakly linking their intensity to the strength of the solar wind. Additionally, we find no significant upper atmosphere responses to magnetic storms, atmospheric evaporation, and other phenomena observed on Mars. By contrasting these results with those from Venus, we highlight key differences in both atmospheres' behavior and their interactions with external forces. We also develop a first-order model to predict 21 cm line intensity variations in both atmospheres based on their gravitational and wind patterns. While this model exhibits promise, it requires further refinement to accurately predict future observations. We anticipate future observations of both planets to shed more light on their atmospheric interactions and potentially open a gateway for interplanetary comparative studies of the atmospheres's electro-magnetic responses. We also suggest several avenues for further investigation into both planetary interactions and the 21 cm line intensity's implications for both Martian and Venusian atmospheric behavior. 

Additionally, we include an appendix detailing our model's code and observations of both planetary atmospheres as well as the data collection and reduction protocols used in this interplanetary comparative study of the atmospheres's electro-magnetic responses.

Formal knowledge acquisition is pivotal for developing artificial intelligence (AI)
capable of human-level cognition, with semantic relationships between entities being
one essential aspect of it. In the realm of Natural Language Processing (NLP), Relation
Extraction (RE), a subset of information extraction, plays a crucial role in acquiring
this vital information from natural language texts. By automatically identifying and
linking related entities within a sentence, RE contributes to the construction of formal
knowledge frameworks, ultimately enriching formal knowledge bases. Nonetheless, RE
poses significant challenges due to the inherent ambiguity of natural language, leading
to a common occurrence of false positive predictions. To mitigate this, sophisticated
techniques are required to validate the extracted relationships, thereby ensuring the
accuracy of formal knowledge acquisition. Motivated by these challenges, this thesis
investigates the potential of utilizing formal argumentation to validate extracted
relationships by incorporating context from a knowledge graph. A novel framework,
RelationFinder, is presented which leverages the capabilities of the knowledge graph to
inform a formal argumentation model. This model employs sentence attributes, along
with related entities and their properties as biasing factors to inform arguments for and
against the extraction of relationships from sentences. A knowledge graph is utilized as
context, providing information to evaluate and assess the relationships extracted from
sentences. System experiments demonstrate that RelationFinder outperforms existing
baselines, achieving substantial reductions in false positive predictions of extracted
relationships. Furthermore, empirical evaluations confirm that RelationFinder's performance
can be benchmarked against that of human extractors, indicating its potential as an
aid to assist human extractors in formal knowledge acquisition. Lastly, the formal
argumentation model utilized in RelationFinder offers a novel and unexplored
approach to addressing the accuracy issues in the realm of RE, contributing to the
general knowledge acquisition pipeline. To date, the knowledge graph used in this
research, along with its corresponding representation as a formal argumentation
model, remains the largest known knowledge graph of its kind, comprising over 1 million
triplets of entities and their associated attributes. Additionally, the source code of
RelationFinder has been made publicly available. It can be accessed at https://github.com/jjj JoyceRelationFinder. This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller closed ball $\Omega_1$, and a first eigenfunction $(u,d)\in H^1_0(\Omega_0)\times\mathbb{R}$ that satisfies homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions on $\Omega_1$ and has zero mean value. A Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem is then formulated as finding $(u,\lambda)\in (H^1_0(\Omega_0)\times\mathbb{R})^m$ that solves $\Delta u = 0$ in $\Omega$ and $u=\lambda h+\int_{\Omega}u^2\,dy$ on $\partial\Omega$, where $\Omega=\Omega_0\setminus\Omega_1$, with $h\geq 0$ and nonconstant, and investigates the associated properties and behaviors of the first eigenvalue. Ultimately, we establish that the first eigenvalue exhibits a minimum and a maximum value, dependant on the given data, and that these extremal functions possess unique symmetry and monotonicity properties. This framework expands upon standard graph theory, offering a more comprehensive approach to modeling complex relationships. Within this framework, we develop methods for identifying clusters of highly interconnected nodes and understanding the dynamics of system interactions. Through statistical analysis, we identify patterns in the hypergraphs that form from random connections and establish a test to evaluate randomness by examining these patterns. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this new approach can shed light on a yet unresolved issue in network science, namely the existence of clusters in a connected graph. Additionally, we present simulations illustrating the effectiveness of this test in distinguishing between random and non-random hypergraphs. In medical radiology reports, doctors document vital information about patients'
health conditions. Their findings are derived from analyzing raw imaging data and
describe the inner body structures. Preparing these reports is labor-intensive and
time-consuming. A system can help streamline this process by automatically extracting
key information from medical images and generating detailed reports. For this system
to be effective, it must be able to understand the context of the images and the
anatomy they show. To overcome this challenge, we propose a system that uses 3D
anatomical structures to plan and guide report generation. By doing so, the system
can ensure that reports are accurate and complete. Here, we present the system's
design and how it addresses the task of report generation. Additionally, we provide
results from experiments using over 6000 scans without manual labels, showing that
the system performs well across different organs. To our knowledge, this system is
the first to use anatomical structures to plan and guide report generation. While
report generation is the focus here, the framework has the potential to support
other tasks as well. In the future, we aim to enhance the system's performance by
incorporating feedback from doctors. This will enable the system to adapt to new
anatomical distributions and improve its overall robustness. Furthermore, we intend
to expand the system's capabilities by supporting a variety of modalities and
organ systems to make it more practical for use in real-world clinical settings.

Our findings provide concrete evidence for the stability of cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. Between 2016 and 2020, the prices of major cryptocurrencies remained steady when compared to other significant financial assets. After isolating shorter price fluctuations lasting less than a month, we analyzed the daily returns in US dollars of leading cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Ripple, alongside their respective counterparts – the Euro and Japanese yen, and major stock indexes, the S&P 500 and MSCI World Index. To evaluate the stability of filtered daily returns, we applied three distinct measures. Firstly, the Pearson correlation coefficients between the analyzed periods showed a notable increase in later years of our study. Secondly, the results of our dynamic time-warping analysis, which permits both leads and lags in relation analysis, demonstrated the existence of similarities in daily returns among cryptocurrencies and their comparators as far back as 2016. Finally, our investigation involved assessing whether cumulative errors in predicting cryptocurrency prices would fall within the predicted bounds as dictated by the Black-Scholes model when considering stable relationships with comparators' daily returns, thereby not refuting the efficient market hypothesis. Additionally, to ensure our conclusions are grounded in an unbiased viewpoint, we performed a comprehensive check for potential data biases. Our research also addresses potential criticisms of previous studies by showcasing the underlying methodology for constructing comparative return indexes and illustrating the method's applicability to other financial markets. Lastly, as our analysis primarily focuses on price stability, our findings do not address the potential for significant, prolonged price drops in cryptocurrencies. In fact, as evidenced by our study's timeframes, such events may occur during our sample period – for instance, the 2017 price surge followed by a significant drop in December 2017. In view of our conclusions, future research could build upon our methodological approach to assess the medium-of-exchange stability of other digital assets and commodity-based cryptocurrencies, such as those based on carbon credits and similar models. Furthermore, our approach could also be extended to investigate the stability of other emerging digital assets and to explore potential similarities with other emerging markets. In addition, as our research did not address the potential for significant, prolonged price drops, future research could shed light on the possibility of such events occurring in cryptocurrencies as a group. In this context, as our sample period includes events such as the 2017 price surge followed by a significant drop in December 2017, an examination of the prices of major cryptocurrencies over an extended period – as long as possible – could provide insights into their future prospects.

a long-standing issue in democracy, yet detecting it has been challenging due to

method combining Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Simulated Annealing to quantify the
level of unfairness in a districting plan. Our results show the effectiveness of
this approach, particularly in a real-world application involving Texas, where a
faster alternative to traditional methods yielded fairer voting distributions and
allowed for the identification of biased districting plans. With an advanced
algorithms in place, we are now capable of efficiently solving large-scale
problems. To facilitate future research, we have made our code available on GitHub.

districts with varying levels of unfairness.

Then, neighboring cells with direction consistency are grouped to enhance the directionality of the GHOG descriptor. Third, a directionality-weighted descriptor is generated by assigning weights to the grouped cells based on their directionality. Our study focuses on how the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons contribute to the radiative decays $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$. The first process is predominantly driven by the $\omega$ meson. On the other hand, the cascade decays involving the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons are substantially suppressed compared to other diagrams, specifically those that go through the $\psi(2S)$ or a three-body decay of $\rho$. Moreover, the $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\gamma$ decay channel, dominated by the $\omega$ meson, yields a branching ratio of approximately $1.53\times 10^{-5}$. Finally, our predicted branching ratios for $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$ range from $1.11\times 10^{-6}$ to $1.14\times 10^{-6}$. The calculated ratios of the $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\gamma$ to $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$ branching ratios vary from $0.0135$ to $0.0137$, largely depending on the treatment of the strong coupling $g_{X\rho\omega}$ between the $X(3872)$, $\rho$, and $\omega$ mesons. The proof involves the analysis of a specific set of linear subspaces within the quadric, and we apply this characterization to investigate the presence of full exceptional collections on certain related varieties, including Grassmannians and quadlinear complete intersections. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per minute, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly 60 times.
On modern hardware, it processes over 18,000 actions per minute, allowing for extensive tests lasting mere days instead of weeks or even months. 
Our analysis reveals that existing evaluation metrics sometimes overestimate agents' performance when using the optimized platform, highlighting the need for revised metrics to accurately assess virtual agents. 
Furthermore, the enhanced framework facilitates the discovery of previously unknown weaknesses in leading agents, such as SAM, which was unable to complete tests in the new environment due to its design limitations. 
Ultimately, our findings underscore the importance of considering the processing power of virtual environments when assessing artificial intelligence.

A key concept called manipulability ellipsoids effectively encodes human pose data and task-dependent information. By using these ellipsoids, robots can learn to mimic human motion or perform specific tasks or actions. However, the ellipsoids' performance heavily depends on the chosen teaching points. For robots mimicking human-like motion, specific focus is on maintaining an upright center of mass to ensure safety and comfort. In contrast, for task-specific robots, teaching points are generally chosen to make the manipulability ellipsoids' principal axes match the target tasks' requirements. A recent breakthrough in deep learning has enabled significant advances in estimating three-dimensional poses from a single two-dimensional image. Most of this progress is attributed to the use of annotated training data, specifically, a large collection of images paired with 2D annotations of real-world object movements. Through conversion to 3D, these annotations facilitate the development of accurate models. A major limitation of this approach, however, lies in the reliance on precise annotations, which are costly and time-consuming to obtain. Consequently, previously, large-scale training datasets have relied on either expensive annotation or smaller, independent projects. In this research, we overcome these challenges by introducing a novel method for automatically extracting accurate annotations from publicly available, 'in-the-wild' video content. In contrast to images, these videos offer the benefit of explicit movement tracking. By leveraging state-of-the-art video processing techniques to isolate moving objects and apply a novel'motion filtering' approach, we are able to eliminate virtually all false positives, enabling reliable conversion to 2D annotations. In turn, these 2D annotations serve as a foundation for the development of a large-scale, single-view 3D object pose estimation model. Experimental results indicate that our approach outperforms all existing models, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the widely used PoseCNN benchmark. Notably, this research marks the first instance of a general, out-of-the-box method successfully applying a single-view 3D object pose estimation model to real-world object movements detected in unannotated, in-the-wild video content. This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A key component of this research involves deriving a new logarithmic blow-up criterion using the method of relative entropy in quantum information theory, as well as the utilization of the Poyed-Björck moving plane technique to analyze the position of solutions over time. Furthermore, this research provides a new understanding of the functional relationships between energy, scattering number, and life span for solutions under the given nonlinearity conditions. Finally, it is shown that solutions with zero energy will remain bounded for all time without experiencing collapse. Conversely, for mass-supercritical focusing nonlinearity in a one-dimensional domain, we prove that solutions with positive energy will eventually experience collapse within a finite time period. This study examines the behavior and simulation of multi-domain ferroelectric FETs by analyzing the oscillations in their electrostatic conduction band profile, which are characteristic of these devices. We model these dynamics by solving coupled two-dimensional Poisson's equations and energy equations for the ferroelectric and semiconductor materials. Our analysis shows that the movement of domain walls within the ferroelectric material leads to the negative capacitance effect, which in turn affects the channel charge and the electrostatic conduction band profile. We also found that near the threshold voltage, the domain wall oscillations can lead to the formation of an inverted profile that shifts towards the gate, resulting in a higher effective effective gate voltage and accelerated channel penetration. This penning effect increases the mobility of electrons and enhances the device's performance. Our simulations show that the combination of both domain penetration and negative capacitance effects optimizes the device's speed while minimizing power loss. Specifically, with a gate voltage of 0.5 V and a voltage of 1.5 V, the domain penetration and negative capacitance can improve the mobility by 25% and 34%, respectively, and the two effects together can boost the drive strength by 45%. This research investigates the prevalence of software security vulnerabilities within popular Rust packages using a variant of code analysis techniques known as dependency analysis. We analyzed 9,714 packages from the Cargo ecosystem, representing the largest and diverse collection of software available in the field. Our study revealed that the Cargo ecosystem hosts 1,519 vulnerable dependencies, accounting for 15.7% of the packages analyzed, with the majority of these vulnerabilities being categorized as memory-related issues (55.6%) or information exposure flaws (26.7%). These security vulnerabilities affect 1,438 maintainers of affected projects, with 50% of these vulnerabilities having public disclosure and 40% being classified as critical in severity. Additionally, we observed that projects incorporating third-party funding or sponsored developers are less likely to contain security vulnerabilities, likely due to increased resources available to maintain these projects. Based on our findings, we recommend that Cargo, the package manager for Rust, introduce enhanced dependency analysis capabilities to alert developers to potential security risks and inform code changes that mitigate these threats. Our research also highlights the importance of transparent disclosure of security vulnerabilities, prompt release of security updates, and clear communication about the maintenance status of projects to enhance software security. By improving software analysis capabilities and promoting a secure Cargo ecosystem, we can create a more secure environment for developers to build and depend on Cargo packages. In the long run, this initiative is expected to contribute to the development of more secure software using Rust. This study seeks to enhance the computational efficiency of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in point cloud learning. We critically examine the conventional graph convolution, and for the first time, identify and quantify its inherent waste of computational resources. We then propose a novel graph convolutional module, GCNet, which optimizes computational efficiency while maintaining equivalent capabilities. The key innovation is a 3D local convolution kernel that efficiently scans nearby points and normal vectors. By replacing the widely used multi-layer perceptron with a efficient linear transformation, we further boost the computational efficiency of GCNet. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that GCNet outperforms state-of-the-art methods in various point cloud learning tasks, including semantic segmentation, semantic segmentation with CAD models, semantic segmentation in video, object detection, and classification, with significantly improved computational efficiency. The code will be publicly available at GitHub. https://github.com/jng6464/GCNet.git. The related data can be found at CSDN. https://blog.csdn.net/semi_srdio. With the increasing popularity of computer vision applications on mobile and embedded devices, optimizing the computational efficiency of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) is crucial for a seamless user experience. However, due to their complex structure, it is challenging to achieve efficiency and effectiveness simultaneously. We propose a novel graph convolutional module, GCNet, which integrates three innovations to significantly enhance the computational efficiency of GCNs while maintaining equivalent effectiveness. First, we identified and quantified the unnecessary computational waste in the multi-layer perceptron used in GCNs, which can be mitigated through a more efficient linear transformation. Next, we developed a 3D local convolution kernel that scans nearby points and normal vectors more efficiently than existing 1D kernels. Finally, I investigated the necessity of incorporating adjacent geometry information in graph convolutional networks via an empirical study, which revealed that these information may cause errors in semantic segmentation. As a result, I proposed a new geometry-invariant graph convolutional network, GCNet, which outperforms existing methods in semantic segmentation while requiring significantly fewer resources. The code is publicly available at GitHub. https://github.com/jng6464/GCNet.git. The data can be found at CSDN. https://blog.csdn.io/semi_srdio. We evaluated GCNet on point cloud learning tasks including semantic segmentation, object detection, and classification, which demonstrated significantly improved computational efficiency without sacrificing effectiveness.
